phpBB CVE-2026-48611 auth bypass: login_link flow with auth_provider=apache AIExploitation High
Hunts the core CVE-2026-48611 exploit request: a POST to /ucp.php driving the OAuth login-link flow (mode=login_link) while forcing auth_provider=apache to skip the password check. This is the single crafted request that logs an attacker into any phpBB account. Rationale: Anchors on the exact PoC request signature (POST /ucp.php + auth_provider=apache + login_link) — auth_provider=apache appearing on the login-link endpoint has no legitimate use, making this near-zero FP. Corroborated by Pentest-Tools and BleepingComputer write-ups of CVE-2026-48611. Cross-checked against: • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phpbb-forum-fixes-auth-bypass-bug-lurking-for-a-decade/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/phpbb-authentication-bypass/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / vuln-management tools (Nessus, Nuclei, Pentest-Tools) actively probing for CVE-2026-48611
  • Internal red-team or pentest engagement replaying the PoC against the forum
  • phpBB plugin/extension that legitimately references a login_link parameter in a POST body (rare)
  • Automated patch-verification scripts that fire the exploit string to confirm 3.3.17 remediation
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !contains "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !contains "Nuclei" and not ipv4_is_in_any_range(SourceIP, "10.0.0.0/8")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP for the window; confirm auth_provider=apache is present and check the HTTP status — a 302 redirect (per PoC) indicates a successful bypass, not just a probe. 2) Contain: if 302/success, block the source IP at the WAF, force-invalidate phpBB sessions (rotate config/session salt or truncate phpbb_sessions), and reset the targeted/admin account credentials. 3) Hunt: from that IP/session pivot to any /adm/ (ACP) or /mcp.php access, new admin-account creation, permission changes, or content/config edits that followed the request.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL contains "/ucp.php"
| where RequestURL contains "auth_provider=apache"
| where RequestURL contains "mode=login_link" or RequestURL contains "login_link_"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

phpBB login_link_* query parameter (CVE-2026-48611 filter-evasion variant) AIExploitation Medium
Catches the defense-evasion form of CVE-2026-48611 where the attacker moves mode=login_link and auth_provider=apache into the POST body so the URL looks like a benign mode=login, while the tell-tale login_link_* dummy query parameter (e.g. login_link_aikido=1) remains in the query string. Rationale: The login_link_* prefix (login_link_aikido=1 in the PoC) is required to make $data non-empty and, per the article's evasion note, survives in the query string even when mode/auth_provider are pushed into the body — a phpBB-specific string with no benign use on /ucp.php POSTs. Cross-checked against: • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phpbb-forum-fixes-auth-bypass-bug-lurking-for-a-decade/
ATT&CKT1078 T1027

  • Vulnerability scanners probing the login-link parameter
  • Pentest replay of the evasion variant
  • phpBB extension exposing its own login_link_* named field
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL !contains "auth_provider=oauth"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, retrieve the POST body if the WAF captures it and check for mode=login_link + auth_provider=apache overriding a mode=login URL; a 302 response indicates success. 2) Contain: block the source and invalidate active phpBB sessions; reset any account whose username matches the submitted login_username. 3) Hunt: correlate the source IP to subsequent authenticated actions (private-message reads, ACP access) and to prior memberlist.php scraping used to pick the target username.

phpBB ACP (/adm/) access shortly after a CVE-2026-48611 bypass request AIInstallation High
Correlates a source that issued the CVE-2026-48611 bypass request (auth_provider=apache on /ucp.php) with that same source reaching the Administration Control Panel (/adm/) within 15 minutes — the privilege-escalation/impact step where an admin-account takeover turns into full forum control. Rationale: Chains the article's exploit signature to the stated impact ('control over the whole forum') by requiring the same source IP that fired the apache-provider bypass to then hit the phpBB ACP (/adm/) or MCP (/mcp.php) within 15 minutes — a temporal correlation that near-eliminates scanner noise since probes rarely follow through to authenticated admin pages. Cross-checked against: • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/phpbb-authentication-bypass/
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator whose workstation shares a NAT egress IP with a scanner that probed the endpoint
  • Pentest engagement where the tester both exploits and then logs into the ACP
  • Shared corporate proxy where an admin and an unrelated probe both appear as the same SourceIP
  • Load-balancer/health-check IP if X-Forwarded-For is not being parsed into SourceIP
Suppression filter
| where not ipv4_is_in_any_range(SourceIP, "10.0.0.0/8") and adminUrl !contains "health"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the ACP access followed the bypass from the same session/IP and was not a known admin's normal login (check csUsername/prior baseline for that IP). 2) Contain: revoke all active admin sessions, reset the admin password and email, and block the source IP; verify no new administrator accounts were created. 3) Hunt: review ACP audit trail for board-config changes, permission-role edits, extension installs, or bulk user/email modifications made from the offending session, and roll back unauthorized changes.
let window = 15m;
let bypass = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestMethod == "POST" and RequestURL contains "/ucp.php" and RequestURL contains "auth_provider=apache" and RequestURL contains "login_link"
    | project bypassTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, bypassUrl = RequestURL;
let admin = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL contains "/adm/" or RequestURL contains "/mcp.php"
    | project adminTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, adminUrl = RequestURL;
bypass
| join kind=inner admin on SourceIP
| where adminTime between (bypassTime .. bypassTime + window)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', adminTime, bypassTime)
| project SourceIP, bypassTime, adminTime, DelaySec, bypassUrl, adminUrl
| sort by bypassTime desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

GitHub Actions runner outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com (tj-actions/changed-files CVE-2025-30066) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a self-hosted CI/CD runner process (Runner.Worker/node/python/curl) reaching gist.githubusercontent.com — the exact egress the compromised tj-actions/changed-files action used to pull its memory-dumping Python second stage. This was StepSecurity Harden-Runner's original detection signal for the March 2025 incident. Rationale: Uses the corroborated network IOC (outbound to gist.githubusercontent.com from a runner) that StepSecurity's Harden-Runner used to detect CVE-2025-30066; scoped to runner process ancestry (Runner.Worker/node/python/_actions paths) to separate it from ordinary developer gist fetches. Cross-checked against CISA, Wiz and Sysdig write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A build step legitimately curls a config/install script hosted on a GitHub gist
  • Developer tooling or dotfiles bootstrap that pulls from gist.githubusercontent.com on a self-hosted runner
  • Package post-install hooks fetching helper scripts from a gist
  • Security tooling / EDR test harness deliberately reaching gist domains
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation resolving raw gist content
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("renovate","dependabot") or RemoteUrl has "raw.githubusercontent.com/your-org")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and parent chain of the initiating process; confirm it ran inside a GitHub Actions job (Runner.Worker/_work/_actions path) and identify the workflow/repo. Grab the exact gist URL and the resolved IP. 2) Contain: if the job used tj-actions/changed-files (or any action pinned to a mutable tag), pause the runner, and immediately rotate every secret exposed to workflows that ran between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC (access keys, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, RSA keys). 3) Hunt: search the same runner fleet for the malicious commit 0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67 and for double-base64 blobs written to workflow logs; review runner egress for other first-seen domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or RemoteUrl has "gist.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","python.exe","python3","python","curl.exe","curl","wget","Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker")
     or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Runner.Worker.exe","Runner.Worker","node.exe","node")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("actions-runner","_work","_actions")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "gist.githubusercontent.com" or HttpHostName in~ ("gist.githubusercontent.com","gist.github.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

tj-actions/changed-files malicious commit 0e58ed86 referenced on host (CVE-2025-30066) AIDelivery High
Alerts on the exact malicious tj-actions/changed-files commit SHA (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67) appearing in any process command line or file path on a self-hosted runner — i.e. the compromised action being fetched, checked out, or pinned. A pure, second-source-confirmed IOC hunt for the retagged supply-chain payload. Rationale: Uses the article's SHA1 (0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67), independently confirmed by CISA and the GitHub Advisory as the single malicious commit every tj-actions/changed-files tag (v1.0.0–v44.5.1) was pointed to — a unique, zero-ambiguity IOC that only appears when the compromised action is fetched, checked out, or SHA-pinned. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/github-actions-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/threat-intel tooling scanning for the hash as an IOC (grep, EDR IOC sweep) surfaces the string in its own command line
  • A remediation script that greps repos/workflows for the malicious SHA
  • Vulnerability-management agent enumerating the commit as data
  • A security researcher reproducing/analyzing the incident in a lab runner
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("grep.exe","findstr.exe","rg.exe","select-string") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC","threat-intel","scan-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA appears in a real action fetch/checkout (Runner.Worker/git/_actions context) versus an analyst's own IOC-scan process; identify the repo and the workflow run time. 2) Contain: treat the runner and any workflow that executed the action as compromised — rotate all secrets exposed to workflows run between 2025-03-12 00:00 and 2025-03-15 12:00 UTC, and repin tj-actions/changed-files to the patched v46.0.1 by full SHA. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound gist.githubusercontent.com egress from the same runner, inspect workflow logs for double-base64 secret blobs, and check for the sibling reviewdog/action-setup CVE-2025-30154 across the fleet.
let ioc = "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67";
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has ioc or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ioc
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessEvent", Account=AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where FolderPath has ioc or FileName has ioc or FolderPath has "tj-actions/changed-files"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", Account=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=FolderPath, Context=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-30066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-30066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or SHA1 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67") or MD5 in~ ("0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google Disrupts NetNut Residential Proxy Network Spanning 2 Million Home Devices

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 7 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Google has significantly degraded NetNut, one of the biggest networks that turns home devices into rented relays for other people's traffic. Working with the FBI, Lumen, and others, Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG)&nbsp;said this week&nbsp;it had reduced the network's pool of usable devices by millions. Google identifies NetNut, also tracked as Popa, as a network spread across home

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Enterprise asset contacting NetNut/Popa residential-proxy gateway (netnut.com/netnut.io) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Enterprise asset contacting NetNut/Popa residential-proxy gateway (netnut.com/netnut.io) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts managed endpoints resolving or connecting to the NetNut (aka Popa) commercial proxy gateway domains named in the article. On a corporate asset this indicates either an embedded NetNut SDK/proxyware component phoning home (turning the host into a rented exit node) or an insider routing traffic through the seized residential-proxy service — neither of which is legitimate enterprise traffic. Rationale: Uses the two concrete IOC domains (netnut.com, netnut.io) named in the article as the only high-fidelity anchor; corroborated by Google Cloud GTIG blog and KrebsOnSecurity confirming NetNut=Popa and the SDK-based exit-node model, though neither disclosed C2 domains/package names, so the gateway domains are the sole reliable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/google-continued-disruption-residential-proxy-networks/ • https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/07/fbi-seizes-netnut-proxy-platform-popa-botnet/ • https://cybernews.com/news/google-fbi-disrupt-netnut-botnet-2-million-devices/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst browsing netnut.com to read the FBI seizure notice
  • Marketing/ad-verification or QA team legitimately evaluating a residential-proxy service for geo-testing
  • Automated URL-detonation sandbox or web crawler visiting the domain from a lab subnet
  • SOC analyst pivoting on the IOC and clicking the domain during triage
  • Corporate DNS resolver forwarding a downstream user's one-off lookup
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process/host — is the connection browser-driven (likely a human visiting the site) or from a non-browser/service process (strong proxyware/SDK signal)? Check whether the host is a managed asset vs a lab/sandbox and whether contacts are repeated/beaconing vs a single lookup. 2) Contain: If a non-browser process is beaconing, isolate the host, block netnut.com/netnut.io and resolved IPs at the proxy/firewall, and quarantine the associated binary for analysis. 3) Hunt: Sweep the environment for the same process hash and for other known bandwidth-sharing/proxyware domains; review the host for unauthorized 'earn-money-for-bandwidth' apps and check whether it acted as an exit node (unexpected inbound/relayed connections) or was co-opted into Mirai/Badbox-style activity.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,10), SampleProc=any(InitiatingProcessFileName), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Connections desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count(), Responses=make_set(DnsResponseName,10) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by Queries desc

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

references:

author: Clankerusecase

logsource:

detection:

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 19 use cases 10 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anubis defense-evasion cluster: Defender RTP disable + Sophos uninstall + PCHunter · [LLM] Anubis pre-ransomware exfiltration tooling egress (rclone, s5cmd, S3 Browser, WinSCP, PuTTY) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Citrix Bleed 2 (CVE-2025-5777) memory over-read via repeated POST to doAuthentication.do AIExploitation High
Hunts the specific CitrixBleed 2 exploitation pattern Anubis affiliates used for initial access: repeated malformed HTTP POST requests to the NetScaler Gateway/AAA endpoint /p/u/doAuthentication.do, each leaking ~126 bytes of appliance memory. A single auth POST is normal; dozens from one source in minutes is the memory-scraping loop. Rationale: Uses the exact article/CVE vector (CVE-2025-5777) and the confirmed exploit endpoint /p/u/doAuthentication.do plus the repeated-POST memory-scrape shape documented by watchTowr and Arctic Wolf; thresholded to separate exploitation from normal auth. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-5777 • https://labs.watchtowr.com/how-much-more-must-we-bleed-citrix-netscaler-memory-disclosure-citrixbleed-2-cve-2025-5777/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/follow-up-updates-on-actively-exploited-information-disclosure-vulnerability-citrix-bleed-2-in-citrix-netscaler-adc-and-gateway-cve-2025-5777/ • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/citrixbleed-vulnerability-detection-mitigation.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate load-balancer/uptime health probes hitting the auth endpoint on a tight interval
  • Automated SSO/MFA retry storms from a broken client pushing repeated auth POSTs
  • Vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable) authenticated-scanning the NetScaler
  • Password-spray tooling (separate TTP) that also loops POSTs to the same endpoint
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known_healthcheck_ip>")   // populate with your LB/monitoring probe IPs; leave empty set if none
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending SourceIP's full request sequence to /p/u/doAuthentication.do; confirm malformed bodies (short Content-Length, login param without value) and check NetScaler build against the CVE-2025-5777 fixed version. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter, terminate active NetScaler ICA/PCoIP sessions, rotate NetScaler session tokens/secrets and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: correlate the source/leaked sessions with subsequent VPN logins, RDP/SMB, and RMM installs on internal hosts; check for AS20473/AS55286 follow-on logins.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC","Gateway")
| where RequestMethod == "POST" and RequestURL has "/p/u/doAuthentication.do"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), UserAgents = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where RequestCount > 15   // each malformed login POST leaks ~126 bytes; a real auth is ~1 POST. 15 = repeated over-read loop
| order by RequestCount desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as request_count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/p/u/doAuthentication.do*" by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where request_count > 15
| sort - request_count
| tstats summariesonly=false count as request_count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/p/u/doAuthentication.do*" by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where request_count > 15
| sort - request_count
The Gentlemen Go backdoor C2 beacon to 81.177.215.15 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts direct outbound connections to the Gentlemen RaaS Go-backdoor C2 (81.177.215.15, TCP/9443) that maintains a bidirectional channel, runs cmd.exe on 'c' bytes and opens a SOCKS proxy on 's' bytes. A hardcoded C2 IP is a high-fidelity single-indicator detection. Rationale: 81.177.215.15:9443 is the exact C2 confirmed by both Kaspersky Securelist and the article; a hardcoded ransomware C2 IP is single-indicator, near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/ • https://expel.com/blog/not-very-gentlemanly-analyzing-a-zero-day-exploit-used-by-the-gentlemen-ransomware-to-disable-targets-edrs/
ATT&CKT1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox/detonation host deliberately contacting the C2
  • Security researcher replaying the sample in a lab that egresses through corporate telemetry
  • Shared-hosting IP re-use if the address is later reassigned to a benign service (verify timestamp vs. campaign window)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("<sandbox_host>")   // exclude sanctioned detonation hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine making the connection and hash the binary - expect an unsigned Go PE in a temp/user path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 81.177.215.15 at egress, kill and preserve the backdoor process/binary for forensics. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same C2 IP and for the sibling ktapi.sys BYOVD driver, PsExec/GPO lateral movement, and any SOCKS-proxy child processes ('s' tasking) pivoting internally.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "81.177.215.15"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "81.177.215.15"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gentlemen BYOVD: vulnerable Kontron ktapi.sys driver dropped/loaded to kill EDR AIInstallation High
Hunts The Gentlemen's BYOVD arsenal: the Kontron ktapi.sys driver (a zero-day, absent from public blocklists) written to disk or loaded to gain kernel access and terminate Microsoft/ESET/Palo Alto/SentinelOne protected processes. ktapi.sys outside a legitimate Kontron install path is high-fidelity. Rationale: ktapi.sys / Kontron is the exact driver named by Expel and the article; because it has no legitimate reason to appear on typical endpoints, filename alone (minus the vendor install path) is a clean high-confidence indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://expel.com/blog/not-very-gentlemanly-analyzing-a-zero-day-exploit-used-by-the-gentlemen-ransomware-to-disable-targets-edrs/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gentlekiller-ransomware-edr-processes/
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Kontron industrial/embedded hardware management software installed under its vendor path (excluded by filter)
  • Driver-research or AV-vendor lab machines intentionally loading vulnerable drivers
  • Backup/imaging of an old system that legitimately shipped the Kontron API
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\Kontron\" and FolderPath !has @"\Program Files\Kontron\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the drop path is NOT a legitimate Kontron directory, hash the driver, and check whether a service was created (7045) and whether EDR agents on the host stopped reporting. 2) Contain: isolate the host, add the ktapi.sys SHA256 to block/deny, and add the driver to the WDAC/HVCI vulnerable-driver blocklist across the fleet. 3) Hunt: look for EDR-process termination immediately after load, the 81.177.215.15 C2, and lateral spread via GPO/PsExec to other hosts staging the same driver.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ktapi.sys"
| where FolderPath !has @"\Kontron\"   // exclude legitimate Kontron API install directory
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "ktapi.sys"
| where TargetFilePath !has "\\Kontron\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DvcAction, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis defense-evasion cluster: Defender RTP disable + Sophos uninstall + PCHunter AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the specific pre-encryption defense-tampering Arctic Wolf tied to Anubis affiliates: disabling Windows Defender real-time protection (Set-MpPreference), running SophosUninstall, and dropping PCHunter to kill/inspect protected processes. Bundled as one detection because the tools co-occur in the same intrusion. Rationale: Maps the three named Anubis evasion artifacts (Defender RTP disablement, SophosUninstall, PCHunter) to concrete binary names and the Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring command; combined as a cluster to raise fidelity above any single tool. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned Sophos migration/decommission where IT runs SophosUninstall
  • Sysadmin toggling Defender RTP during legitimate software packaging/troubleshooting
  • Endpoint engineering testing PCHunter for benign kernel/driver inspection
  • Automated AV-swap scripts during managed fleet rollouts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-sccm","svc-intune") and AccountName !in~ ("svc-avmgmt")   // exclude sanctioned endpoint-management service accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the account/host is an authorized IT admin doing sanctioned AV maintenance (check change ticket) vs. an unexpected user/session, and whether it was RDP/PsExec-spawned. 2) Contain: isolate the host, re-enable Defender RTP, block PCHunter hash, and preserve process artifacts. 3) Hunt: if unauthorized, look for immediate follow-on ktapi.sys BYOVD, shadow-copy deletion, RMM install and exfil tooling on the same host - the Anubis pre-encryption sequence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("PCHunter.exe","PCHunter64.exe","SophosUninstall.exe")
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Set-MpPreference" and ProcessCommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring")
   or (FileName =~ "MpCmdRun.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "RemoveDefinitions")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(TargetUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName has_any ("\\PCHunter.exe","\\PCHunter64.exe","\\SophosUninstall.exe"))
   or (NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Set-MpPreference" and CommandLine has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis remote-access staging: cloudflared tunnel + non-baseline RMM agents AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the persistence/C2 layer Arctic Wolf tied to Anubis: a Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared run with 'tunnel') plus the specific legitimate RMM agents abused to blend in (MeshAgent, Remotely, UltraVNC, ScreenConnect, Zoho Assist). cloudflared 'tunnel' on a server is the sharpest element; RMM binaries add context. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's named tooling (cloudflared tunnel + MeshAgent/Remotely/UltraVNC/ScreenConnect/Zoho Assist); cloudflared 'tunnel' on servers is rarely legitimate, RMM binaries scoped to hosts where they are not the sanctioned tool. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1219 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organization officially using ScreenConnect/Zoho Assist/MeshCentral as its sanctioned RMM (whitelist those hosts)
  • Developer legitimately running cloudflared tunnel to expose a dev service
  • IT deploying UltraVNC/MeshAgent as its standard remote-support agent
  • Cloudflare Zero Trust connector installed as an approved access solution
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("<sanctioned_rmm_host1>")   // exclude hosts where the RMM/cloudflared is the approved tool
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the RMM/cloudflared binary is your sanctioned tool and whether install was via an approved deployment channel or dropped ad-hoc into a temp/user path; review the cloudflared tunnel target. 2) Contain: kill the tunnel/agent, block the associated *.cloudflare/argotunnel egress, and remove the unauthorized RMM. 3) Hunt: pivot to preceding VPN/RDP access, PsExec service creation, and downstream exfil tooling (rclone/s5cmd) on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel")
   or FileName in~ ("MeshAgent.exe","Remotely_Agent.exe","winvnc.exe","ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe","ZA_Connect.exe","ZohoURSService.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetProcessName endswith "\\cloudflared.exe" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "tunnel")
   or TargetProcessName has_any ("MeshAgent.exe","Remotely_Agent.exe","winvnc.exe","ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe","ZA_Connect.exe","ZohoURSService.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis pre-ransomware exfiltration tooling egress (rclone, s5cmd, S3 Browser, WinSCP, PuTTY) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the data-theft-before-encryption stage: the specific transfer/exfil utilities Arctic Wolf tied to Anubis (rclone, s5cmd, S3 Browser, WinSCP, PuTTY/pscp/psftp) reaching public destinations. Pairs the named binaries with public egress so it flags exfil rather than benign internal file moves. Rationale: Uses the exact exfil toolset named by Arctic Wolf; the Defender variant is gated on public-IP egress to distinguish S3/SFTP exfil from benign internal transfers, keeping it deployable as a hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ransomware-groups-turn-to-citrix-bleed.html
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admins legitimately using WinSCP/PuTTY for routine SFTP file management to known partners
  • DevOps using rclone/s5cmd for sanctioned S3/backup sync jobs
  • Data teams uploading to approved cloud storage buckets
  • Scheduled backup tasks invoking these utilities on servers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-backup","svc-devops") and not (RemoteUrl has_any ("<approved_bucket_endpoint>"))   // exclude sanctioned backup/DevOps flows
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the command line for the destination (bucket/host/keys) and volume; confirm whether the account and destination are sanctioned. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host, block the egress destination, revoke any embedded cloud/SFTP credentials, and preserve the tool + config. 3) Hunt: correlate with prior credential access, RMM/cloudflared presence, and imminent ransomware indicators (shadow-copy deletion, encryptor drop then self-delete) to determine if exfil preceded encryption.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rclone.exe","s5cmd.exe","WinSCP.exe","pscp.exe","psftp.exe","putty.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "s3browser"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("rclone.exe","s5cmd.exe","WinSCP.exe","pscp.exe","psftp.exe","putty.exe","s3browser")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/

    - attack.credential-access

    category: process_access
    product: windows

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

ARToken/EvilTokens PhaaS infrastructure contact (pamconj.com panel + Cloudflare Worker lure) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network connections to the specific ARToken operator-panel and phishing-lure domains published by Talos (dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev). A host resolving/connecting to these means a user reached the device-code phishing lure or operator infrastructure — the earliest on-wire signal of this M365 token-theft campaign. Rationale: Uses the three concrete Talos-published IOC domains plus the pamconj.com apex to catch sibling operator subdomains. These are dedicated malicious infrastructure, so any resolution is high-fidelity; cross-checked against Talos, Sekoia and Microsoft reporting of the same EvilTokens/ARToken infra. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/01/eviltokens-device-code-phishing-kit-totally-more-evil-than-we-all-thought/5265409
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team detonating the lure URL in a sandbox/SOAR enrichment from a corporate endpoint
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing to pamconj.com during investigation
  • Web proxy/URL-scanner appliance pre-fetching the domain for categorization
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ appliance logging the blocked query (benign but noisy)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/device and confirm whether the connection was a live browser navigation (device-code lure) vs automated scanner; pull the referring email/Teams message for the same recipient. 2) Contain: block all *.pamconj.com and the workers.dev lure at proxy/DNS; if a real user reached the device-code page, revoke that user's refresh tokens/sessions (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken) and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (new Entra device registration for that user) and UC3 (inbox-rule creation) within 24h; review that user's SigninLogs for device-code grants from unfamiliar IPs.

| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DvcHostname
