Entra ID device registration = ARToken PRT persistence after device-code token theft AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ARToken/EvilTokens persistence step: after stealing a refresh token via device-code phishing, the operator registers a new device in Entra ID to obtain a Primary Refresh Token for durable SSO that survives password resets. Surfaces device add/register/join audit events with the acting user, source IP and target device for rapid correlation to a suspicious sign-in. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit 'Primary Refresh Token (PRT) persistence' capability and corroborated by Sekoia/Microsoft describing refresh-token-driven device registration in Entra ID. Device add/register audit operations are the concrete, queryable footprint of that step; Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because Entra ID audit isn't in FDR or CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/microsoft-365-phishing-panel-uses-oauth-device-code-flow/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user enrolling a new phone/laptop into Intune/Entra (BYOD or refresh cycle)
  • Autopilot/Intune bulk device provisioning by IT during onboarding
  • Windows Hello for Business device registration on password change
  • Service desk registering a replacement device for a user
Suppression filter
| where ActorIp !in ("<intune_provisioning_egress_ip>")  // NOTE: replace only if you maintain a known Intune egress allowlist; otherwise correlate ActorIp against SigninLogs device-code/foreign-IP sign-ins
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each registration confirm the actor UPN, source IP and device name; check whether the user's most recent sign-in was a device-code grant or came from an unfamiliar/foreign IP within the prior hour. 2) Contain: if unattributable, disable/remove the newly registered device, revoke the user's refresh tokens and PRTs (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken + session invalidation), and require MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: enumerate all devices registered by the same actor IP across the tenant, review SharePoint/OneDrive mass-download and inbox-rule creation (UC3) for the affected mailbox.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("Add registered owner to device","Add registered users to device","Register device","Add device")
| extend Ip = tostring(IPAddress)
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, Ip, CountryCode, City, ObjectName, ObjectType
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Add registered owner to device","Add registered users to device","Register device","Add device","Update device")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend TargetDevice = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIp, TargetDevice, Result, ResultReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ARToken BEC toolkit: inbox forwarding/hiding rule creation on compromised M365 mailbox AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the ARToken/EvilTokens post-compromise BEC action: automated creation of inbox rules that forward/redirect mail externally and delete or move messages to hide attacker activity. Targets mailbox audit events for New/Set-InboxRule carrying forwarding or delete/move parameters. Rationale: Directly targets ARToken's documented BEC capability ('inbox rule creation for forwarding and deleting messages') via the exact Exchange audit operations and forwarding/delete parameters. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty because M365 mailbox audit isn't shipped to those platforms in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberscoop.com/artoken-bec-platform-cisco-talos/ • https://gbhackers.com/eviltokens-linked-artoken-panel/
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately setting up out-of-office/auto-forward to a personal or delegate mailbox
  • Admin-configured transport/journaling rule mistaken for a user inbox rule
  • Power-user creating a 'move to folder' organization rule for newsletters
  • Migration tooling recreating rules during a mailbox move
Suppression filter
| where Params !has "@yourcorpdomain.com"  // keep only rules forwarding/redirecting OUTSIDE the org; internal delegate forwarding is common and low-risk
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the rule forwards/redirects to an EXTERNAL domain or deletes/moves security-alert mail; check the ClientIP/country against the user's normal sign-in pattern and recent device-code sign-ins. 2) Contain: delete the malicious rule, revoke the user's tokens and PRTs, reset credentials, and block the external forwarding destination at the mail gateway. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (infra contact) and UC2 (new device registration) for the same user; search for identical rule names/forwarding targets across other mailboxes to scope the BEC blast radius.

| where RawEventData has_any ("ForwardTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo","RedirectTo","DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend Params = tostring(Parameters)
| where Params has_any ("ForwardTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo","RedirectTo","DeleteMessage","MoveToFolder")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Params, OfficeWorkload
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")

          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

It is small permissions, weak checks, open systems, and normal tools doing things they were allowed to do. That same pattern runs

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: AI Compute Hijacking, Apple Email Flaw, BlueHammer Ransomware + 14 S
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BeepRAT (DCRat variant) HFY.exe telephone-utility masquerade + scheduled-task persistence · [LLM] Platform-aware phishing: Ninite Loader deploying ConnectWise ScreenConnect RAT · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BeepRAT DNS-over-HTTPS C2 resolution from non-browser process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
BeepRAT (DCRat variant) HFY.exe telephone-utility masquerade + scheduled-task persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts the BeepRAT infection chain where a ZIP-delivered .NET binary named HFY.exe poses as a Chinese phone-number management tool and establishes persistence via scheduled tasks. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact masquerading binary name and the parent->schtasks persistence pivot Rubrik documented for this China-nexus campaign. Rationale: Anchors on the exact binary HFY.exe named by Rubrik Zero Labs plus the documented scheduled-task persistence mechanism; HFY.exe is a non-generic name so the FP surface is tiny. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine third-party build literally named HFY.exe (legitimate Chinese telephone-management tool) installing itself
  • Software-deployment tooling where an unrelated app named HFY.exe spawns schtasks during setup
  • Developer/QA running a self-compiled .NET utility named HFY.exe
  • Packaging/repackaging labs testing archived Chinese-language utilities
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Program Files\\" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of HFY.exe and check it against VT/ThreatFox; inspect the schtasks command line for the task name, trigger and the executable it points to, and confirm the file originated from a ZIP in a Downloads/Temp path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable/delete the created scheduled task, and quarantine HFY.exe plus its bundled third-party DLLs. 3) Hunt: sweep the estate for the same SHA256/task name and pivot to UC2 (DoH C2) to see if the host already resolved and beaconed to C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "HFY.exe"
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HFY.exe" and FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\HFY.exe"
    or (ParentProcessName endswith "\\HFY.exe" and NewProcessName has_any ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: BeepRAT HFY.exe Masquerade and Scheduled Task Persistence
id: 6f3b1c2e-4d5a-4e8b-9c1a-2f7d8e0a1b34
description: Detects the BeepRAT (DCRat variant) telephone-utility binary HFY.exe executing or spawning scheduled-task/persistence children
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html
  - https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/03
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_hfy:
    Image|endswith: '\HFY.exe'
  selection_task:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\HFY.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\schtasks.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
  condition: selection_hfy or selection_task
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\HFY.exe OR *\\hfy.exe OR *\\HFY.EXE) OR (@ParentImage:(*\\HFY.exe OR *\\hfy.exe) AND @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\cmd.exe)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/\\HFY\.exe$/i OR (ParentBaseFileName=/HFY\.exe/i ImageFileName=/(schtasks|powershell|cmd)\.exe$/i))
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="HFY.exe" OR (Processes.parent_process_name="HFY.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="HFY.exe" OR (Processes.parent_process_name="HFY.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
BeepRAT DNS-over-HTTPS C2 resolution from non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts BeepRAT's covert C2 resolution, where a non-browser process (e.g. HFY.exe / .NET host) resolves attacker infrastructure via DNS-over-HTTPS to public DoH resolvers on 443, bypassing local DNS logging before beaconing. Article-specific because BeepRAT's distinguishing tradecraft is DoH-based C2 lookup rather than plaintext DNS. Rationale: Uses BeepRAT's documented DoH-based C2 resolution (Rubrik) plus the non-browser-process constraint to convert generic DoH traffic into a targeted hunt; the article's extracted domain api.service.bio could not be corroborated by a second source so it is deliberately excluded from the filter (behavioral DoH pivot only). Sentinel lacks a clean process-name field on network telemetry, so its version surfaces host/DoH pairs without the process filter. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-ai-compute-hijacking-apple.html • https://zerolabs.rubrik.com/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1090 T1620
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browsers configured with 'Secure DNS' pointed at Cloudflare/Google (some enterprise policies force this outside the browser exe list)
  • Endpoint security / content-filter agents that perform DoH resolution natively
  • Windows 11 built-in DoH client (svchost) — excluded but variants may slip through
  • Privacy tooling / VPN clients that proxy DNS over HTTPS
  • Developer tools testing DoH endpoints
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Program Files\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","SenseNdr.exe","NisSrv.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and its folder path; if it is HFY.exe, an unsigned .NET host, or a binary in Downloads/Temp, treat as high priority and pull its SHA256. 2) Contain: isolate the host and block the resolved C2 (capture it from a full packet/proxy log if available since DoH hides the query). 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (HFY.exe / scheduled task) on the same host and pivot for in-memory .NET assembly loads, webcam/screenshot/keylog artifacts, and any proxy-launch behavior BeepRAT supports.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemotePort == 443
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","dns.quad9.net","doh.opendns.com","one.one.one.one","dns.nextdns.io","doh.cleanbrowsing.org")
    or RemoteIP in ("1.1.1.1","1.0.0.1","8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4","9.9.9.9","149.112.112.112")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","svchost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Connections=count(), any(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstPortNumber == 443
| where DstHostname has_any ("cloudflare-dns.com","dns.google","dns.quad9.net","doh.opendns.com","one.one.one.one","dns.nextdns.io","doh.cleanbrowsing.org")
    or DstIpAddr in ("1.1.1.1","1.0.0.1","8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4","9.9.9.9","149.112.112.112")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Connections=count() by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr
| sort by FirstSeen desc

references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationPort: 443
    DestinationHostname:
      - '*cloudflare-dns.com'
      - '*dns.google'

  condition: selection and not filter_browsers

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:443 (@DestinationHostname:(*cloudflare-dns.com OR *dns.google OR *dns.quad9.net OR *doh.opendns.com) OR @DestinationIp:(1.1.1.1 OR 1.0.0.1 OR 8.8.8.8 OR 8.8.4.4 OR 9.9.9.9)) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\MsEdge.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\opera.exe OR *\\iexplore.exe)

Platform-aware phishing: Ninite Loader deploying ConnectWise ScreenConnect RAT AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Cofense-documented platform-aware phishing chain where User-Agent fingerprinting delivers a 'Ninite Loader' to Windows victims that then installs ConnectWise ScreenConnect (repurposed as a RAT). Article-specific because it pivots on the Ninite-loader parent spawning a ScreenConnect client dropped from a browser/download path rather than generic RMM usage. Rationale: Uses Cofense's documented chain (Ninite Loader -> ConnectWise ScreenConnect RAT) with the parent-loader/download-path constraint to separate phishing-delivered ScreenConnect from sanctioned RMM deployments; ScreenConnect binary names and the &e=Access&y=Guest session marker are high-signal when combined with an untrusted parent. Cross-checked against: • https://cofense.com/blog/the-platform-you-trust-is-the-platform-they-target • https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/phishing-campaigns-auto-adapt-victims-device-os
ATT&CKT1219 T1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned IT helpdesk installing ConnectWise ScreenConnect for legitimate remote support
  • MSP onboarding pushing ScreenConnect agents to managed endpoints
  • A user legitimately downloading ScreenConnect from a vendor portal into their Downloads folder
  • Genuine ninite.com installer bundling remote-support tooling
  • Security team red-team exercises deploying ScreenConnect
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Program Files\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientSetup.exe")) and ProcessCommandLine !has "<your-sanctioned-relay-host>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether ScreenConnect is a sanctioned RMM in your estate; if so, verify the relay/instance host in the command line matches your tenant and the parent is your deployment tool, not Ninite/Downloads/Temp. 2) Contain: if the relay is unknown/attacker-controlled, isolate the host, kill the ScreenConnect.ClientService, and block the relay FQDN/IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pull the delivering email/URL and check UrlClickEvents for the fingerprinting landing page, then sweep for Itarian RAT installs and other hosts contacting the same relay.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl")
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "ScreenConnect"
    or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ConnectWise"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "&e=Access&y=Guest"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "Ninite"
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl") or CommandLine has "&e=Access&y=Guest"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\Ninite.exe"
    or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\Downloads\\","\\Temp\\","\\Users\\Public\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)

10 Layers Deep: How StepSecurity Stops TeamPCP's Trivy Supply Chain Attack on GitHub Actions

StepSecurity
2026-07-02 7 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

TeamPCP weaponized 76 Trivy version tags overnight. The KICS attack followed the same playbook days later. One security control is not enough. Here is how the StepSecurity platform's ten independent security layers work together to prevent credential exfiltration, detect compromised actions at runtime, and respond to incidents across your entire organization before attackers can succeed.

CVEsCVE-2026-33634
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1555.003
Domainsscan.aquasecurtiy.org checkmarx.zone models.litellm.cloud audit.checkmarx.cx tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io
IPs45.148.10.212 83.142.209.203 94.154.172.43

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TeamPCP sysmon.py systemd persistence beaconing ICP canister C2
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TeamPCP Trivy stealer C2/exfil egress to typosquat & Checkmarx/LiteLLM domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] CI stealer reads /proc/<pid>/mem to scrape secrets from Runner.Worker
TeamPCP Trivy stealer C2/exfil egress to typosquat & Checkmarx/LiteLLM domains AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from CI runners or developer hosts to the TeamPCP credential-stealer infrastructure used in the trivy-action/KICS compromise: the typosquat exfil domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org and its hardcoded IPs, plus the checkmarx/litellm lookalike domains. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact typosquatted C2 named in the writeup rather than generic beaconing. Rationale: Anchors on the exact typosquat exfil domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org and its resolved IP 45.148.10.212 plus the sibling checkmarx.zone/litellm/ICP-canister domains — all confirmed by Microsoft, CrowdStrike and Wiz writeups, not just the original article, making these hard, low-FP IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/from-scanner-to-stealer-inside-the-trivy-action-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher or blue-teamer deliberately visiting scan.aquasecurtiy.org during IOC validation from a sandbox host
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment tooling that DNS-resolves IOC domains for reputation scoring
  • Legitimate traffic to the real aquasecurity.com — verify the misspelled 'aquasecurtiy' before dismissing
  • A canister proxy (raw.icp0.io) used by an unrelated legitimate ICP/Web3 application on a developer workstation
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (InitiatingProcessCommandLine/ContextImageFileName) that made the connection and whether the host is a CI runner running aquasecurity/trivy-action, setup-trivy, or the Checkmarx KICS action; confirm the domain spelling is the typosquat. 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at egress, isolate the runner/job, and immediately rotate every secret the job could touch (AWS/GCP/Azure tokens, SSH keys, kube configs, GITHUB_TOKEN/PAT). 3) Hunt: pin all Actions to full commit SHAs, search other runners for /proc/*/mem reads (UC2) and sysmon.py ICP beacons (UC3), and check for an attacker-created public repo named 'tpcp-docs' holding exfil release assets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud","tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io")
    or RemoteIP in ("45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocDomains = dynamic(["scan.aquasecurtiy.org","checkmarx.zone","audit.checkmarx.cx","models.litellm.cloud","tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io"]);
let iocIPs = dynamic(["45.148.10.212","83.142.209.203","94.154.172.43"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImNetworkSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DstIpAddr in (iocIPs) or DstHostname in~ (iocDomains) or Url has_any (iocDomains)
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery in~ (iocDomains)
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamPCP Trivy/KICS Stealer C2 or Exfil Domain Resolution
id: 8f3c1e42-9b77-4d2a-a1c6-2f0e5d7a4b91
description: Detects DNS resolution of the TeamPCP credential-stealer typosquat/C2 domains used in the trivy-action and Checkmarx KICS supply chain compromise (CVE-2026-33634).
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/10-layers-deep-how-stepsecurity-stops-teampcps-trivy-supply-chain-attack-on-github-actions
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/03
tags:

  - attack.t1071.001

detection:

      - scan.aquasecurtiy.org
      - checkmarx.zone
      - audit.checkmarx.cx
      - models.litellm.cloud
      - tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io
  condition: selection
level: high
source:linux.auditd (@process.command_line:(*scan.aquasecurtiy.org* OR *checkmarx.zone* OR *audit.checkmarx.cx* OR *models.litellm.cloud* OR *raw.icp0.io*) OR CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 45.148.10.212/32, 83.142.209.203/32, 94.154.172.43/32))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(scan\.aquasecurtiy\.org|checkmarx\.zone|audit\.checkmarx\.cx|models\.litellm\.cloud|tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai\.raw\.icp0\.io)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action, bytes
| filter dstAddr in ["45.148.10.212", "83.142.209.203", "94.154.172.43"]
| stats sum(bytes) as totalBytes, count(*) as flows by srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action
| sort totalBytes desc

CI stealer reads /proc/<pid>/mem to scrape secrets from Runner.Worker AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the TeamPCP stealer's in-memory credential harvesting: a non-debugger process (a spawned Python interpreter) reading /proc/<pid>/mem to extract marked secrets from the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process. This is the exact behavior the article and Microsoft/CrowdStrike describe and is highly anomalous on a build runner. Rationale: The /proc/<pid>/mem read is the precise credential-harvesting behavior named in the article ('read /proc/pid/mem of the Runner.Worker process') and independently confirmed by Microsoft and CrowdStrike; one process reading another's memory image is near-zero on a legitimate build runner. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/from-scanner-to-stealer-inside-the-trivy-action-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Interactive debugging with gdb/lldb attaching to a live process during troubleshooting
  • CRIU checkpoint/restore or container-runtime (containerd/runc) live-migration reading process memory
  • Legitimate memory-forensics or profiling tooling (e.g. process dumpers) run by a developer
  • A self-referential process reading its OWN /proc/self/mem (lower risk — pivot on cross-PID reads)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gdb","lldb","criu","containerd","runc") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("gdb","lldb")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reader is not gdb/criu/containerd and that the target PID belongs to Runner.Worker or another secret-holding process; capture ProcessCommandLine and parent (should trace back to a Trivy/KICS action step). 2) Contain: kill the job, isolate the runner, and rotate all secrets exposed to that workflow (cloud tokens, SSH keys, GITHUB_TOKEN/PAT, kube configs). 3) Hunt: check the same host for egress to the TeamPCP C2 domains (UC1) and the sysmon.py ICP beacon (UC3), and review which repos/workflows referenced aquasecurity/trivy-action or Checkmarx KICS by mutable tag.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","dd","cat","gcore")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Proc Filesystem Memory Scraping of Another Process (/proc/PID/mem)
id: 2a7d9c15-4e83-4b1f-9a20-6c8f3d1e70ab
description: Detects a process opening /proc/<pid>/mem, the memory-scraping technique the TeamPCP stealer used to pull secrets from the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process during the trivy-action compromise.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/10-layers-deep-how-stepsecurity-stops-teampcps-trivy-supply-chain-attack-on-github-actions
  - https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/from-scanner-to-stealer-inside-the-trivy-action-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/03
tags:
  - attack.t1003.007
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|re: '/proc/[0-9]+/mem'
  filter_debug:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/gdb'
      - '/lldb'
      - '/criu'
      - '/containerd'
  condition: selection and not filter_debug
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:*/proc/* AND @process.command_line:*/mem*) -@process.executable.path:(*/gdb OR */lldb OR */criu OR */containerd)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/\/proc\/[0-9]+\/mem/
| ContextImageFileName=/(python|python3|dd|cat|gcore)/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(gdb|lldb|criu|containerd)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

TeamPCP sysmon.py systemd persistence beaconing ICP canister C2 AIInstallation High
Hunts the TeamPCP persistence stage: a masquerading sysmon.py systemd service that beacons an Internet Computer (ICP) blockchain canister (tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io) roughly every 50 minutes for C2 instructions after the malicious Trivy binary runs. Article-specific via the exact canister domain and sysmon.py masquerade on Linux (where Sysmon does not exist). Rationale: Anchors on the exact ICP canister C2 domain (tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai.raw.icp0.io) from the article's IOC list plus the sysmon.py systemd masquerade — both confirmed by Wiz and SANS as the persistence/beacon stage; a Linux host resolving this specific canister on a ~50-min cadence is unambiguous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/trivy-compromised-teampcp-supply-chain-attack • https://www.sans.org/blog/when-security-scanner-became-weapon-inside-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1071.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer workstation running a legitimate Internet Computer / Web3 application that proxies through raw.icp0.io canisters
  • Security tooling resolving the canister domain during IOC validation or sandbox detonation
  • A genuine host-based 'sysmon' Linux port (rare) unrelated to the malware — verify the .py masquerade and beacon cadence
  • Threat-intel enrichment pipelines that DNS-resolve the canister for reputation scoring
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","curl","wget") or SampleCmd has "sysmon.py"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving host also ran the malicious Trivy binary (v0.69.4) or a compromised action, and inspect /etc/systemd/system and /lib/systemd for a sysmon.py-referencing unit plus the ~50-min beacon periodicity. 2) Contain: disable and remove the rogue systemd service, kill the sysmon.py process, block *.raw.icp0.io canister egress, and rotate all credentials the host held. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same canister resolutions and for the C2/exfil domains (UC1) and /proc/*/mem reads (UC2); verify no downstream CanisterWorm-tainted npm packages were installed from the same credentials.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai" or RemoteUrl endswith "raw.icp0.io"
| summarize BeaconCount=count(), DistinctMinutes=dcount(bin(Timestamp,1m)), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where BeaconCount >= 2   // repeated ~50-min poll, not a one-off visit
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "tdtqy-oyaaa-aaaae-af2dq-cai" or DnsQuery endswith "raw.icp0.io"
| summarize Beacons=count(), DistinctHours=dcount(bin(TimeGenerated,1h)), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, DnsQuery, SrcUsername
| where Beacons >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ConsentFix lure delivery: inbound email link to DocSend/Dropbox or ConsentFix phishing infra · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ConsentFix: interactive browser sign-in to Azure CLI / dev-tool first-party app · [LLM] ClickFix: PowerShell/mshta download-execute spawned from Run dialog (explorer parent) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ConsentFix: Azure CLI token redemption from divergent IP within 10 min of interactive sign-in · [LLM] Post-session-theft mailbox abuse: auto-forwarding / inbox rule creation via stolen M365 session · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ConsentFix: interactive browser sign-in to Azure CLI / dev-tool first-party app AIExploitation High
Hunts the core ConsentFix token-theft primitive: a normal user completing an interactive browser OAuth sign-in to Azure CLI (or Azure PowerShell / VS Code / Visual Studio / Teams PowerShell) first-party apps. These developer tooling apps are near-never used interactively via a browser by regular staff, so the event is the fingerprint of the localhost-callback consent lure described in the article. Rationale: Uses the concrete first-party ApplicationIds confirmed by Push Security / Mitiga / gblock as the apps ConsentFix abuses (Azure CLI 04b07795-... is a public client, so the auth code alone yields tokens). Interactive browser sign-in to CLI/dev tooling by ordinary users is the high-fidelity anomaly. Localhost callback mechanic cross-checked against the consentfix-phishing-page screenshot and Push Security write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/consentfix • https://www.mitiga.io/blog/consentfix-oauth-phishing-explained-how-token-based-attacks-bypass-mfa-in-microsoft-entra-id • https://www.gblock.app/articles/consentfix-v3-azure-cli-oauth-microsoft-365-phishing • https://detection.fyi/elastic/detection-rules/integrations/azure/initial_access_entra_id_oauth_phishing_via_first_party_microsoft_application/
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or cloud/DevOps engineer legitimately running `az login` with the interactive browser flow
  • IT admin authenticating to Azure PowerShell via browser during troubleshooting
  • VS Code Azure extension sign-in by a developer
  • GitHub Codespaces / Cloud Shell auth redeeming codes for a genuine user
  • First-time Azure onboarding session for a new cloud engineer
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("devbox","jumpbox") and AccountUpn has_any ("svc-","admin-"))   // exclude known dev/admin workstations after per-tenant tuning
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether the signed-in user is in a role that legitimately uses Azure CLI/PowerShell (DevOps, cloud eng). Check IPAddress/Location/UserAgent against the user's baseline and whether a localhost callback error immediately preceded on the endpoint. Step 2 (contain): If unexpected, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset and re-MFA, and review/remove any app consents granted. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on AccountObjectId for a non-interactive token redemption from a different IP within 10 minutes (UC2), and check for new mailbox forwarding/inbox rules and Graph enumeration from the same session.
let VulnerableFirstPartyApps = dynamic(["04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56","04f0c124-f2bc-4f59-8241-bf6df9866bbd","12128f48-ec9e-42f0-b203-ea49fb6af367"]);
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationId in (VulnerableFirstPartyApps)   // Azure CLI + dev-tool public clients abused by ConsentFix
| where IsInteractive == true
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ClientAppUsed == "Browser"                    // interactive browser flow = the lure, not native CLI use
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, Browser, DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
let VulnerableFirstPartyApps = dynamic(["04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56","04f0c124-f2bc-4f59-8241-bf6df9866bbd","12128f48-ec9e-42f0-b203-ea49fb6af367"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AppId in (VulnerableFirstPartyApps)
| where IsInteractive == true
| where ResultType == 0
| where ClientAppUsed == "Browser"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, AppDisplayName, AppId, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by TimeGenerated desc
