Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Inbound exploitation of Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF (CVE-2026-20230) from campaign infra · [LLM] Cisco Unified CM SSRF file:// arbitrary file-write payload (CVE-2026-20230)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue Apache Axis AdminService / JSP webshell on Cisco Unified CM (CVE-2026-20230 post-exploit)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Inbound exploitation of Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF (CVE-2026-20230) from campaign infra AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the Cisco Unified CM WebDialer service that carry SSRF exploit markers (file://, Apache Axis AdminService) or originate from the Defused-reported campaign IP 156.146.38.167. This is the initial-access step Cisco confirmed is under active exploitation. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated exploit chain (WebDialer service + Apache Axis AdminService + file:// SSRF) confirmed by Cisco's advisory, SOCRadar and DarkReading; the campaign IP 156.146.38.167 is currently single-source (Defused) so it is used as a booster, not the sole anchor. Defender/Falcon left empty because CUCM is a Linux Tomcat appliance not onboarded to EDR — detection lives on the wire (CEF) and in appliance syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/less-than-24-hours-attackers-weaponize-cisco-cucm-flaw
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDialer click-to-call SOAP traffic from internal CTI/UC applications (will lack file:// and AdminService markers)
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) probing the WebDialer endpoint from a known scan subnet
  • Internal penetration-test or Cisco TAC-guided validation of the patch from a corporate source IP
  • Security-team replaying the public PoC from a sanctioned research host
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has "webdialer" and not (RequestURL has_any ("file://","file:/","AdminService","/axis/")) and SourceIP !in (CampaignIPs))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is a Unified CM host and inspect the full RequestURL for a file:// scheme or Axis AdminService call; check whether WebDialer is enabled and whether the CUCM version predates 14SU6/15SU5. 2) Contain: block SourceIP 156.146.38.167 at the perimeter, disable the WebDialer service (Cisco's interim mitigation), and restrict WebDialer to trusted management networks. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same DestinationIP for follow-on /axis/ AdminService requests and newly created .jsp files under the Tomcat web root (see webshell UC), and review CUCM install/security logs for unexpected files.
let CampaignIPs = dynamic(["156.146.38.167"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has "webdialer"
| where SourceIP in (CampaignIPs)
   or RequestURL has_any ("file://", "file:/", "AdminService", "/axis/", "%2Ffile", "%66%69%6c%65")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction, RequestClientApplication
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Unified CM SSRF file:// arbitrary file-write payload (CVE-2026-20230) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to a Unified CM host whose URI/query embeds a file:// scheme, the mechanism Defused observed attackers using to write attacker-controlled files onto the appliance via the WebDialer SSRF. Content-pivot detection independent of source IP. Rationale: Uses the article's specific technique string 'properly constructed file:// payloads to create files' plus the corroborated Axis/WebDialer target paths; matches on request content so it fires regardless of rotating source IPs. URL-encoded variants included because SSRF payloads are commonly percent-encoded to bypass filters. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/ • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW
ATT&CKT1190 T1105
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners injecting file:// test strings during authorized SSRF assessments
  • WAF/IPS logging the raw payload of a blocked request (verify DeviceAction shows block, not allow)
  • Developers or Cisco TAC reproducing the PoC in a lab that shares the SIEM
  • Legitimate application passing a file: parameter unrelated to CUCM (excluded by the webdialer/axis/ccmadmin path requirement)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction !in~ ("blocked","denied","drop","reset")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the file:// path in RequestURL to see what the attacker attempted to read/write, and confirm whether the WAF allowed or blocked (DeviceAction). 2) Contain: if allowed, isolate the CUCM host from untrusted networks, disable WebDialer, and snapshot the appliance for forensics before patching to 14SU6/15SU5. 3) Hunt: search the same host for follow-on /axis/services/AdminService calls and newly written .jsp files, and review CUCM audit logs for unexpected OS-level files created around the request timestamp.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("webdialer", "/axis/", "/ccmadmin/")
| where RequestURL has_any ("file://", "file:%2F%2F", "file:/", "%66%69%6c%65%3a")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue Apache Axis AdminService / JSP webshell on Cisco Unified CM (CVE-2026-20230 post-exploit) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the post-SSRF stage where attackers invoke the Apache Axis AdminService on the CUCM Tomcat stack to deploy a rogue SOAP service and then access an attacker-dropped .jsp webshell in the web root — the code-execution/persistence tail of the CVE-2026-20230 chain. Rationale: Targets the corroborated post-exploit chain (SOCRadar/DarkReading: rogue Apache Axis service deployed via AdminService, then a JSP file-writer/command shell in the Tomcat web dir). AdminService invocation and new .jsp access on a production CUCM are highly abnormal, giving a sharp signal distinct from the initial SSRF request. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/less-than-24-hours-attackers-weaponize-cisco-cucm-flaw • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-20230-cisco-unified-cm-webdialer-ssrf/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cisco built-in .jsp application pages accessed during normal CCMAdmin/Self-Care usage (baseline the specific known .jsp set)
  • Cisco upgrade/COP file installation touching Tomcat webapps
  • Authorized admin using legitimate Axis-based CUCM management functions from a management host
  • Vulnerability scanner fingerprinting the /axis/ path
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL contains ".jsp" and DestinationHostName !has "cucm" and RequestURL !has "AdminService")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact .jsp path and whether it exists in a stock CUCM image; a non-catalog .jsp or any external-sourced GET/POST to /axis/services/AdminService is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the CUCM host, capture the .jsp and Tomcat logs, and treat the appliance as root-compromised — plan rebuild/restore rather than in-place cleanup. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the originating SSRF file:// request and source IP, review outbound connections from the CUCM host for C2/reverse shell, and check for credential/config exfiltration and lateral movement from the appliance.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/axis/services/AdminService", "AdminService", "/axis/services")
   or (RequestURL contains ".jsp" and RequestURL has_any ("/webdialer/", "/axis/", "/ccmadmin/", "/cucm-uds/"))
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

CISA: Microsoft SharePoint RCE flaw now actively exploited

BleepingComputer
2026-07-02 6 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

CISA warned on Wednesday that attackers have begun exploiting a high-severity Microsoft SharePoint remote code execution vulnerability patched in May. [...]

CVEsCVE-2026-45659
ATT&CKT1190 T1486
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
Detected

Weaponization
—
Phase 3
Delivery

Phase 4
Exploitation
Detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawns shell/LOLBIN — CVE-2026-45659 deserialization RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SharePoint worker (w3wp.exe) writes .aspx web shell into LAYOUTS web root — CVE-2026-45659 post-exploit
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawns shell/LOLBIN — CVE-2026-45659 deserialization RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the code-execution step of the CVE-2026-45659 SharePoint deserialization RCE: the gadget chain runs in the context of the SharePoint application-pool worker (w3wp.exe), which then spawns a command interpreter or LOLBIN. A production SharePoint server's IIS worker process essentially never spawns cmd/powershell/certutil, so this is high-fidelity for exploitation. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core claim that CVE-2026-45659 lets an authenticated attacker 'execute code remotely on the SharePoint Server' via deserialization; corroborating write-ups (Akamai, Trellix, Rapid7) confirm the payload runs as the w3wp.exe app-pool identity, and w3wp spawning cmd/powershell is the canonical exploitation signal for SharePoint deserialization RCE. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/microsoft-patches-sharepoint-rce-flaw.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/05/26/sharepoint-vulnerability-cve-2026-45659/ • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/sharepoint-vulnerability-rce-active-exploitation-detections-mitigations • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-zero-day-exploitation-of-microsoft-sharepoint-servers-cve-2025-53770/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint timer/health scripts or admin PSConfig runs that spawn cmd/powershell under the STS/app-pool context during patching
  • Monitoring agents (SCOM, custom probes) invoking net.exe or whoami.exe under the IIS worker for health checks
  • Backup or DLP integrations that shell out from a custom SharePoint web part
  • Non-SharePoint IIS sites sharing a w3wp.exe binary name where a web app legitimately shells out
  • Post-patch validation tooling that queries app-pool identity via whoami
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig", "Microsoft.SharePoint.Administration") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a SharePoint server and pull the full child command line + SHA256; look for encoded/download strings, machine-key/web.config reads, or recon (whoami/net). Check whether the CVE-2026-45659 May 2026 update (SharePoint 2016/2019/Subscription Edition) is installed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the server from the network, kill the offending process tree, and preserve w3wp memory/IIS logs; if compromise confirmed, rotate the SharePoint MachineKey/ASP.NET keys (stolen keys enable forged-request persistence). 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (web-shell writes into LAYOUTS), review IIS logs for the originating authenticated account and source IP, and sweep other internet-exposed SharePoint servers for the same w3wp child-spawn pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\whoami.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SharePoint w3wp.exe Spawning Shell or LOLBIN (CVE-2026-45659 Deserialization RCE)
id: 8f2b1c4d-6a7e-4b3f-9c21-5d8e0a1f7b62
status: experimental
description: Detects the SharePoint IIS application-pool worker (w3wp.exe) spawning a command interpreter or LOLBIN, the code-execution step of the CVE-2026-45659 deserialization RCE.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-microsoft-sharepoint-rce-flaw-now-actively-exploited/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/microsoft-patches-sharepoint-rce-flaw.html
  - https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/sharepoint-vulnerability-rce-active-exploitation-detections-mitigations
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\w3wp.exe'
    Image|endswith:

      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'

      - '\wscript.exe'

| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|mshta|wscript|cscript|rundll32|regsvr32|certutil|bitsadmin|curl|net|net1|whoami)\.exe$/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="w3wp.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
SharePoint worker (w3wp.exe) writes .aspx web shell into LAYOUTS web root — CVE-2026-45659 post-exploit AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step after CVE-2026-45659 exploitation: the SharePoint IIS worker process writing a new web-accessible handler (.aspx/.ashx/.asmx) into the SharePoint LAYOUTS/Web Server Extensions directory. Legitimate SharePoint provisions these files via the installer/solution deployment, not from the live w3wp worker at runtime — so a runtime write here is a strong web-shell indicator. Rationale: The article states CVE-2026-45659 grants RCE with the SharePoint process's permissions; corroborating SharePoint-RCE research (Akamai, Trellix, Rapid7) shows attackers immediately drop .aspx web shells into the LAYOUTS web root (C:\Program Files\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\Web Server Extensions\..\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS\), and a runtime write of a new handler by w3wp.exe is not legitimate SharePoint behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/sharepoint-vulnerability-rce-active-exploitation-detections-mitigations • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-zero-day-exploitation-of-microsoft-sharepoint-servers-cve-2025-53770/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/microsoft-patches-sharepoint-rce-flaw.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint cumulative-update / PSConfig deployment writing provisioned .aspx pages into LAYOUTS during patching windows
  • WSP solution package deployment (Add-SPSolution/Install-SPSolution) staging application pages
  • Third-party SharePoint add-ins provisioning custom application pages at first activation
  • Admin manual copy of a legitimate application page authored under the app-pool account
  • Antivirus/DLP quarantine-restore operations rewriting an existing .aspx in place
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig", "Install-SPSolution", "Add-SPSolution", "stsadm"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve and read the written file — a short/obfuscated page with eval/Request/Process.Start or MachineKey/web.config access is a web shell; note file SHA256, path, and timestamp, and confirm the May 2026 CVE-2026-45659 patch state. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the server, quarantine/remove the file (retain a copy), kill any live w3wp child process tree, and rotate SharePoint MachineKey/ASP.NET machine keys since forged-request persistence survives file removal. 3) HUNT: Correlate to UC1 (w3wp spawning shells), search IIS logs for POST requests immediately preceding the file write to identify the authenticated account and source IP, and sweep all SharePoint servers for other recently written handlers in LAYOUTS.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS\" or FolderPath has @"\Web Server Extensions\"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asmx"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName endswith "w3wp.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS\" or TargetFilePath has @"\Web Server Extensions\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".aspx" or TargetFileName endswith ".ashx" or TargetFileName endswith ".asmx"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI Agent Exploits Langflow RCE to Automate Database Ransomware Attack

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 19 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Security firm&nbsp;Sysdig&nbsp;says it has found what it believes is the first ransomware attack run from start to finish by an AI agent. Its Threat Research Team calls the operator JADEPUFFER and says a large language model handled the whole job: breaking in, stealing credentials, moving deeper into the network, then encrypting and wiping a company's production database. Ransomware has always

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2025-3248) via /api/v1/validate/code POST · [LLM] Langflow web service (uvicorn/gunicorn/python) spawning shell or download tool · [LLM] Nacos auth bypass (CVE-2021-29441) via 'User-Agent: Nacos-Server' to create rogue admin · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Cron/systemd persistence beaconing to JADEPUFFER C2 45.131.66.106 · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JADEPUFFER C2 beacon to 45.131.66.106:4444/beacon · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Database ransomware impact: README_RANSOM table / ransom-note strings + mass DROP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Langflow unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2025-3248) via /api/v1/validate/code POST AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POST requests to the Langflow code-validation endpoint that CVE-2025-3248 abuses for unauthenticated Python execution, the exact entry vector JADEPUFFER used. Article-specific because it pins the named CVE's documented vulnerable endpoint on an internet-facing Langflow box rather than a generic web exploit. Rationale: Pins CVE-2025-3248's documented vulnerable endpoint (/api/v1/validate/code) + POST, the exact unauthenticated-RCE path the article names as JADEPUFFER's way in. Defender left empty because MDE does not ingest reverse-proxy/web access logs; endpoint manifestation is covered by the execution UC. WebSearch was blocked in this session so no external corroboration could be pulled.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow flow authors saving/validating custom Python components
  • Internal CI/CD or health-check jobs POSTing to the validate endpoint
  • Security scanners / ASM tools probing the known CVE path
  • Blue-team CVE-2025-3248 validation testing
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "HealthCheck" and SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the request body/user-agent and source IP; confirm whether the payload contains exec/import/os/subprocess and whether the Langflow build is <1.3.0 (still vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the Langflow instance off the public internet, and rotate every API key/cloud credential reachable from its environment. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a child shell/interpreter spawned by uvicorn/gunicorn/python, beacons to 45.131.66.106, and new cron persistence.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/validate/code"   // CVE-2025-3248 Langflow code-exec endpoint
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow web service (uvicorn/gunicorn/python) spawning shell or download tool AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the on-host manifestation of the Langflow RCE: the web-service process spawning a shell, curl, or wget to run recon and sweep secrets (MinIO minioadmin default, cloud keys) and reach the staging server 64.20.53.230. Article-specific because a Langflow/uvicorn parent spawning /bin/sh is the RCE payload firing, not normal app behaviour. Rationale: A public-facing Langflow/uvicorn process spawning /bin/sh or curl is the RCE detonating; enriched with the article's concrete secret-sweep artifacts (minioadmin default cred, staging IP 64.20.53.230, cloud-provider key names). WebSearch blocked so no second-source confirmation; grounded in article body.
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow custom components that legitimately shell out to system tools
  • In-container entrypoint scripts where python/uvicorn launches a shell at startup
  • Ops using curl/wget from an app-service context for package or model downloads
  • Health-check or exporter sidecars spawning shell probes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("entrypoint.sh","docker-entrypoint") and FileName in~ ("sh","bash"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line for recon (id, uname, env), credential paths (.aws/credentials, minioadmin), or egress to 64.20.53.230. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Langflow process tree, and rotate all secrets that lived in that environment (OpenAI/Anthropic/DeepSeek/Gemini keys, AWS/Azure/GCP/Alibaba/Tencent creds). 3) Hunt: pivot to network events for 45.131.66.106 and 64.20.53.230, and check for a new cron job beaconing every 30 minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn","gunicorn","python","python3","langflow","node")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| extend SecretSweep = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("minioadmin","64.20.53.230","credentials",".aws","OPENAI","ANTHROPIC","DEEPSEEK")
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("uvicorn","gunicorn","python","python3","langflow","node")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget")
| extend SecretSweep = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("minioadmin","64.20.53.230","credentials",".aws")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SecretSweep
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JADEPUFFER C2 beacon to 45.131.66.106:4444/beacon AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any connection to the JADEPUFFER command-and-control IP 45.131.66.106, the target of a /beacon check-in on port 4444 every 30 minutes. Article-specific: a dedicated, published malicious IP + port + URI from Sysdig's IOC list. Rationale: 45.131.66.106 is Sysdig's published JADEPUFFER C2 IP with a documented :4444/beacon check-in every 30 minutes; a dedicated malicious IP makes any hit high-fidelity. WebSearch was blocked so the IOC is taken directly from the article's Sysdig indicator list without independent second-source confirmation.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation infrastructure deliberately touching the IOC
  • Blue-team IOC-validation connectivity tests
  • A benign service that later gets assigned the same recycled VPS IP (verify timeframe)
  • Security scanner sweeping the /24 that includes this IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process/context making the connection (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) and whether check-ins recur near a 30-minute cadence. 2) Contain: block 45.131.66.106 (and staging 64.20.53.230) egress at perimeter, isolate the beaconing host. 3) Hunt: on that host enumerate cron/systemd timers, look for the Langflow RCE parent-child chain, and check MySQL/Nacos hosts for README_RANSOM tables and dropped databases.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "45.131.66.106"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "45.131.66.106"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cron/systemd persistence beaconing to JADEPUFFER C2 45.131.66.106 AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence mechanism: a scheduled job (cron/crond/atd) launching curl/wget/shell that contacts 45.131.66.106, the article's 'scheduled task that pinged the attacker's server every 30 minutes.' Distinct from the raw network IOC because it pivots on the scheduler parent, catching the persistence even if the beacon lands intermittently. Rationale: Combines the article's 30-minute scheduled-task persistence with the concrete C2 IP 45.131.66.106, pivoting on the cron parent so the persistence is caught even between beacon hits. WebSearch blocked; IOC and behaviour taken from the article/Sysdig indicators only.
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned monitoring cron jobs that curl an external endpoint (verify the IP)
  • Admin-authored heartbeat scripts to a legitimate host that shares the /24
  • Backup/telemetry agents scheduled via cron reaching out on interval
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the cron entry (crontab -l, /etc/cron.d/*, /var/spool/cron) and confirm the target IP and 30-minute cadence. 2) Contain: remove the malicious cron/systemd unit, block 45.131.66.106 egress, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to the Langflow RCE process chain and to any MySQL/Nacos host showing README_RANSOM or dropped tables; check for a MinIO server still on minioadmin default creds.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond","atd")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.131.66.106"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cron","crond","atd")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "45.131.66.106"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nacos auth bypass (CVE-2021-29441) via 'User-Agent: Nacos-Server' to create rogue admin AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to Nacos user-management endpoints carrying the User-Agent 'Nacos-Server' identity that CVE-2021-29441 abuses to bypass authentication and add an admin account, exactly what JADEPUFFER did before encrypting the config store. Article-specific: named CVE + Nacos default-signing-key takeover leading to a planted admin. Rationale: Uses CVE-2021-29441's well-known bypass signature — the spoofed 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent hitting /nacos/v1/auth/users to add an admin — which the article names as JADEPUFFER's Nacos takeover step. Defender/Falcon/Datadog empty because this is a web-request artifact those EDR/FDR feeds don't carry. WebSearch was blocked, so no external corroboration was obtained.
ATT&CKT1190 T1136.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Nacos cluster nodes using the Nacos-Server identity for inter-node calls (baseline internal peer IPs)
  • Security testing of the Nacos CVE by the blue team
  • Misconfigured client library that copies the Nacos-Server user-agent
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !startswith "10." and SourceIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/non-cluster and check whether a new Nacos user/admin was created around that time. 2) Contain: take Nacos off the public internet, rotate the default signing key, remove rogue admin accounts, and stop it connecting to its DB as root. 3) Hunt: check the backing MySQL for a README_RANSOM table and dropped tables, and correlate with the Langflow RCE host and C2 45.131.66.106.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestClientApplication has "Nacos-Server"   // CVE-2021-29441 identity-bypass User-Agent
| where RequestURL has "/nacos/v1/auth/users"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Nacos CVE-2021-29441 Authentication Bypass User Creation

Database ransomware impact: README_RANSOM table / ransom-note strings + mass DROP AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on JADEPUFFER's impact stage — creation of the README_RANSOM ransom table, presence of the ransom Bitcoin address / Proton contact, or a root-context mysql client issuing DROP TABLE/DROP DATABASE after the Nacos config store was encrypted. Article-specific via three unique published strings. Rationale: Three unique published IOCs — ransom table README_RANSOM, Bitcoin address 3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy, contact e78393397@proton.me — plus root-context mysql DROP make this near-zero-FP and specific to the JADEPUFFER impact stage. WebSearch was blocked so these strings are taken from the article's Sysdig indicator list without a second source.
ATT&CKT1486 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA restoring/testing on a lab copy who names a table README_RANSOM while investigating the IOC
  • Threat-hunt queries themselves logging the IOC strings into command lines
  • Legitimate scheduled DROP TABLE cleanup jobs (verify not root-from-internet and no ransom strings)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "threat-hunt" and AccountName != "dba-restore-svc"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the README_RANSOM table / note and whether DROP/TRUNCATE ran under the DB root account; identify the source session and host. 2) Contain: isolate the DB server, revoke internet exposure of the DB admin account, and preserve logs — note the actor claims AES but printed the key once and never saved it, so recovery from backups is the only path. 3) Hunt: trace back to the Nacos auth-bypass and Langflow RCE hosts, block C2 45.131.66.106 and staging 64.20.53.230, and audit MinIO for the minioadmin default login.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
    or (FileName in~ ("mysql","mysqladmin") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DROP TABLE","DROP DATABASE","TRUNCATE"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
    or (SyslogMessage has_all ("DROP","TABLE") and SyslogMessage has "root")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JADEPUFFER Database Ransomware Impact Strings

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Mass execution of binaries from SYSVOL/NETLOGON (abused GPO software distribution)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PurpleFox in-memory install: msiexec.exe fetching a remote MSI · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Missed incidents, persistent threats, and response gaps: Insights from compromis
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] LionTail IIS backdoor: unexpected DLL written to / loaded by an IIS worker (w3wp) · [LLM] Web-server process (w3wp/httpd) spawning a command shell or LOLBin · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Remote management tool executing from a non-install (temp/download) path · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Long-lived cryptomining C2 (stratum) from SYSTEM context on servers / domain controllers · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Long-lived cryptomining C2 (stratum) from SYSTEM context on servers / domain controllers AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the article's four-year-old cryptomining case study: unsigned miners running as SYSTEM on servers/DCs beaconing to mining pools over stratum/getwork ports for weeks or longer. Focuses on persistent SYSTEM-context egress to pool infrastructure rather than a single connection. Rationale: Anchored on the explicit 'four-year-old crypto mining activity on domain controllers' case study; stratum pool ports + SYSTEM/machine-account context + >7-day persistence is the high-fidelity combination the article says endpoint tools missed. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1496/
ATT&CKT1496 T1569.002 T1547.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain/validator node software on a lab server
  • Approved GPU-render or scientific-compute jobs using pool-like ports
  • Security tools port-scanning internal ranges hitting these ports
  • Monitoring agents polling on 5555/7777 for app telemetry
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary path/signature and whether the host is a DC or server; pull FirstSeen — multi-week SYSTEM egress on a DC is near-certain TP. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the miner process, and capture the scheduled task/service/Run-key that relaunches it before removal. 3) Hunt: pivot on the pool IP/domain across all hosts, review the same persistence mechanism enterprise-wide, and check DC event logs for the original install time (may predate current retention).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemotePort in (3333,4444,5555,7777,14433,14444,45700,45560)
     or RemoteUrl has_any ("stratum","xmr","monero","minexmr","nanopool","supportxmr","miningpool","pool.min")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("system","local service","network service") or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), Dsts=make_set(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where datetime_diff('day', LastSeen, FirstSeen) >= 7   // persistence beyond a week = the miner-on-DC pattern
| order by FirstSeen asc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstPortNumber in (3333,4444,5555,7777,14433,14444,45700,45560)
     or Url has_any ("stratum","xmr","monero","minexmr","nanopool","supportxmr","miningpool")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber), Dsts=make_set(DstIpAddr) by DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcUsername
| where datetime_diff('day', LastSeen, FirstSeen) >= 7
| order by FirstSeen asc
title: Cryptomining Pool Connection on Stratum Ports
id: 4a1e2f90-3c7b-4d61-9a2e-77c1b5d9a001
description: Outbound connection to common cryptomining pool ports, matching the multi-year miner-on-DC case study
references:
  - https://securelist.com/compromise-assessment-findings-2025/120542/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1496
  - attack.impact
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationPort:
      - 3333
      - 4444
      - 5555
      - 7777
      - 14433
      - 14444
      - 45700
      - 45560
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationPort:(3333 OR 4444 OR 5555 OR 7777 OR 14433 OR 14444 OR 45700 OR 45560) OR @DestinationHostname:(*stratum* OR *xmr* OR *monero* OR *nanopool* OR *supportxmr* OR *minexmr*))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| RemotePort=/^(3333|4444|5555|7777|14433|14444|45700|45560)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
| count >= 1
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_port IN (3333,4444,5555,7777,14433,14444,45700,45560) OR All_Traffic.app IN ("stratum","stratum+tcp")) by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | eval durDays=(lastTime-firstTime)/86400 | where durDays >= 7 | sort - durDays
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_port IN (3333,4444,5555,7777,14433,14444,45700,45560) OR All_Traffic.app IN ("stratum","stratum+tcp")) by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | eval durDays=(lastTime-firstTime)/86400 | where durDays >= 7 | sort - durDays
PurpleFox in-memory install: msiexec.exe fetching a remote MSI AIExploitation High
Hunts the article's in-memory PurpleFox case study. PurpleFox uses msiexec.exe to download and execute its remote MSI stage (often with a randomized/.moe/.png extension), then injects via PowerShell and hides with a rootkit. Catches the on-disk pivot the fileless payload cannot avoid: msiexec reaching out to a URL. Rationale: PurpleFox is named in the article as an in-memory infection that evaded endpoint protection; external write-ups (Trend Micro, AhnLab) confirm msiexec-fetches-remote-MSI as its signature install step — a reliable on-disk pivot for an otherwise fileless chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/19/i/purple-fox-fileless-malware-with-rookit-component-delivered-by-rig-exploit-kit-now-abuses-powershell.html • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/55492/
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1055 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise software deployment tools staging MSIs from an internal HTTP repo
  • SCCM/Intune app installs pointing at an internal distribution URL
  • Vendor installers that chain a web-hosted MSI
  • Admin manually installing from a trusted download link
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sccm","configmgr","intune") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the URL host and MSI reputation; internal repo = likely benign, unknown external host = escalate. Check for a child powershell.exe or wmiprvse injection within 60s. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the URL/host at proxy, and snapshot memory before reboot (rootkit hides on-disk artifacts). 3) Hunt: search for the same URL/MSI hash org-wide, look for hidden Run keys and driver services (rootkit persistence), and review SMB auth failures indicating worm-style spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" /i"," -i","/q",".moe",".msi",".png")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
title: Msiexec Installing MSI From Remote URL (PurpleFox pattern)
id: 4a1e2f90-3c7b-4d61-9a2e-77c1b5d9a002
description: msiexec.exe invoked with an http/https URL to fetch a remote package, matching the in-memory PurpleFox install chain

  - https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/19/i/purple-fox-fileless-malware-with-rookit-component-delivered-by-rig-exploit-kit-now-abuses-powershell.html

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\msiexec\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/https?:\/\//i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process_name="msiexec.exe" (Endpoint.Processes.process="*http://*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*https://*") by Endpoint.Processes.dest, Endpoint.Processes.user, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | sort - firstTime

LionTail IIS backdoor: unexpected DLL written to / loaded by an IIS worker (w3wp) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the in-memory LionTail case study on critical Windows servers. LionTail (Scarred Manticore) installs as a DLL via search-order hijacking into IIS/web-server processes and talks to http.sys directly. Surfaces non-standard DLLs dropped into web dirs or loaded by w3wp.exe from outside the OS/inetsrv trees. Rationale: LionTail is named as an in-memory infection on critical Windows servers; Check Point/SecurityWeek confirm its install-as-DLL-into-IIS-via-search-order-hijacking + http.sys behavior, so DLLs appearing in inetpub/inetsrv or loaded by w3wp from odd paths is the article-specific pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2023/from-albania-to-the-middle-east-the-scarred-manticore-is-listening/ • https://www.securityweek.com/iranian-cyber-spies-use-liontail-malware-in-latest-attacks/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web-app deployment copying custom .NET assemblies into inetpub
  • IIS module/extension installs (URL Rewrite, ARR) dropping DLLs
  • Developer publishing a site directly to the server
  • AV/EDR agents loading their own DLLs into w3wp for inspection
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the DLL's signer, hash reputation, and export table; an unsigned, unknown DLL loaded by w3.exe on an internet-facing server is high-priority. 2) Contain: isolate the server, capture a memory image (LionTail is memory-resident), and preserve IIS logs before remediation. 3) Hunt: enumerate http.sys URL ACLs (netsh http show urlacl) for rogue prefixes, review IIS access logs for the backdoor's configured URL paths, and check other web servers for the same DLL name/hash.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName endswith ".dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\" and FolderPath !has @"\inetsrv\" and FolderPath !has @"\Microsoft.NET\" and FolderPath !has @"\assembly\" and FolderPath !has @"\Temporary ASP.NET Files\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ModulePath=FolderPath, ModuleName=FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\inetpub\", @"\inetsrv\")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","tiworker.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
title: DLL Written Into IIS Web Directory (LionTail side-load)

Web-server process (w3wp/httpd) spawning a command shell or LOLBin AIInstallation High
Hunts two article findings at once: web shells restored from backups (40% of discovered web shells lived in backups) and LionTail-style remote command execution. Web-server worker processes spawning cmd/powershell/net/whoami is the canonical web-shell / server-backdoor command-exec signal. Rationale: Directly targets the article's web-shell-in-backups finding and LionTail remote-command execution; a web worker spawning cmd/powershell/net has near-zero legitimate cause and re-fires the moment a backdoored backup is restored. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web app legitimately shelling out to a build/deploy script
  • Monitoring plugins that call whoami/systeminfo for health checks
  • Custom .NET app using System.Diagnostics.Process to run net.exe
  • Admin troubleshooting an app pool via an interactive shell under the IIS account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","\\deploy\\","msdeploy") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line for recon/tasking (whoami, net user, download cmdlets); pull the web access logs around the timestamp for the requesting IP and URL/aspx/php path. 2) Contain: quarantine the web-shell file, isolate the host, and revoke the app-pool identity's cached tickets. 3) Hunt: scan web roots AND backup images for aspx/aspx/php/jsp files with recent write times or eval/exec patterns (the 40% that hide in backups), and block the source IP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","php-cgi.exe","tomcat.exe","tomcat9.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","systeminfo.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ChildProcess=FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","php-cgi.exe","tomcat.exe","tomcat9.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","systeminfo.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

Mass execution of binaries from SYSVOL/NETLOGON (abused GPO software distribution) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the 'overly permissive GPO-based software distribution' case study. Detects executables/scripts launched directly from the replicated SYSVOL/NETLOGON share across many domain members near-simultaneously — the fingerprint of malware pushed via a tampered logon/startup GPO script. Rationale: Directly grounded in the GPO-distribution case study; legitimate GPO logon scripts run from SYSVOL but a NEW unsigned binary executing from SYSVOL across 5+ hosts is exactly the 'goes wrong' scenario, and the cross-host count separates a real push from a one-off. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1484/001/
ATT&CKT1484.001 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate, approved logon/startup scripts running an installer from SYSVOL
  • A sanctioned software rollout that was genuinely pushed via GPO
  • Login scripts calling cscript/wscript for drive mapping
  • Admin testing a new GPO script across a pilot OU
Suppression filter
| where not (SHA256 in (dynamic([])) )
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the binary/script and its SHA256; verify against approved GPO scripts and check the file's signer and SYSVOL write time. 2) Contain: pull the offending file from SYSVOL, disable/edit the GPO delivering it, and force gpupdate to stop further spread. 3) Hunt: review DC Directory Service and File Replication logs for who modified the GPO script, check gPCFileSysPath ACLs for over-permissive write rights, and sweep endpoints that already executed it.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\SYSVOL\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\SYSVOL\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" or FolderPath has @"\NETLOGON\"
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","cmd.exe")
| summarize Hosts=dcount(DeviceName), HostList=make_set(DeviceName, 25), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 5) by FileName, SHA256, FolderPath
| where Hosts >= 5   // 5+ domain members running the same SYSVOL-sourced binary = mass GPO push
| order by Hosts desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\SYSVOL\" or CommandLine has @"\SYSVOL\" or CommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" or NewProcessName has @"\NETLOGON\"
| summarize HostCount=dcount(Computer), Hosts=make_set(Computer, 25), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by NewProcessName, CommandLine
| where HostCount >= 5
| order by HostCount desc
title: Process Executed From SYSVOL or NETLOGON Share

Remote management tool executing from a non-install (temp/download) path AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the article's 'legitimate yet suspicious' RMM finding — RMM tools appeared in every engagement that led to a detection. Flags known RMM agents launched from temp/download/ProgramData/public paths rather than their normal Program Files install location, indicating attacker-dropped remote access. Rationale: Grounded in the article's finding that RMM tools appeared in every incident-producing engagement; scoping to execution from temp/download/public paths (not Program Files) turns an otherwise-noisy RMM inventory into a high-fidelity attacker-dropped-RMM signal. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Help-desk running a portable AnyDesk/TeamViewer from Downloads for one-off support
  • MSP agent (Atera/Syncro) legitimately staging in ProgramData
  • User self-installing RustDesk from their Downloads folder
  • Portable RMM binary in a software-testing sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe") and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the RMM tool is sanctioned for this host/user; check the incoming connection ID/email in the RMM client and the parent process that launched it. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, kill the agent, block its cloud endpoints at the proxy, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same RMM binary across the estate, review outbound connections to the vendor's relay infrastructure, and correlate with new local accounts or scheduled tasks created around the same time.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("anydesk.exe","teamviewer.exe","screenconnect.clientservice.exe","atera_agent.exe","ateraagent.exe","splashtop.exe","strwinclt.exe","rustdesk.exe","meshagent.exe","netsupport.exe","client32.exe","dwagent.exe","logmein.exe","gotoassist.exe","supremo.exe","syncro.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("anydesk.exe","teamviewer.exe","screenconnect.clientservice.exe","atera_agent.exe","ateraagent.exe","splashtop.exe","strwinclt.exe","rustdesk.exe","meshagent.exe","netsupport.exe","client32.exe","dwagent.exe","logmein.exe","gotoassist.exe","supremo.exe","syncro.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\Temp\\","\\Downloads\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Users\\Public\\","\\AppData\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),

| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified")
      AND (Filesystem.file_path="*C:\Windows\Fonts\Mysql*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*C:\Windows\System32\wbem*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/dev/null*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/var/folders/*" OR Filesystem.file_name IN ("nei.bat","dl1host.exe","bat.bat","cmd.bat","taskhost.exe","poab.bat","load.bat","loab.bat","mance.exe","eter.exe","puls.exe","eternalblue2.dll","doublepulsar2.dll","http.sys","scrcons.exe"))
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]
| append [
  | tstats summariesonly=false count
      from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
      where Registry.action IN ("created","modified")
        AND (Registry.registry_path="*HKU\\S-1-5-21-*" OR Registry.registry_path="*HKLM\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall*" OR Registry.registry_path="*HKLM\\Software\\WOW6432Node\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall*")
      by Registry.dest, Registry.process_name, Registry.registry_path,
         Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.registry_value_data
  | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
]

Azure AD MFA push-bombing / fatigue burst followed by successful sign-in (Scattered Spider) AIExploitation High
Hunts Scattered Spider's signature MFA-fatigue vector: a burst of >=10 denied/failed MFA challenges against one account inside 5 minutes, immediately followed by a successful MFA sign-in (the moment the fatigued user finally taps Approve). Article-specific to the collective's 'targeted MFA bombing (aka MFA fatigue)' technique. Rationale: Directly implements the article's 'targeted MFA bombing (aka MFA fatigue)' phrase using the canonical Entra push-denial codes (500121 auth-failed-during-MFA, 50074 MFA-required, 50076/50072) with a >=10-in-5-min burst gated by a subsequent MFA success — the fatigue-approval moment. CISA AA23-320A confirms push-bombing/MFA-fatigue as a primary Scattered Spider MFA-bypass method. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1621 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit user whose phone lost connectivity retrying MFA repeatedly then succeeding
  • Misconfigured mobile mail client looping token refresh and generating repeated MFA prompts
  • Conditional Access policy change causing a wave of re-auth prompts across a device
  • New device enrollment where the user fumbles several approvals before accepting
  • Shared/service account with automation re-prompting MFA on session expiry
Suppression filter
| where SuccessIP != tostring(DeniedIPs[0])   // drop bursts where the eventual success came from an already-seen prompt IP (real user retry)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the DeniedIPs vs SuccessIP for the account — different geo/ASN between the denial burst and the success is strong TP; same-IP retries are usually the real user. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken), force re-registration of MFA, and temporarily block sign-in if geo mismatch. 3) Hunt: for confirmed accounts, review AuditLogs for MFA method additions, inbox-rule creation, and role assignments in the 6h after the success, and check other accounts hit by burst prompts from the same source IP.
let MfaDenied = dynamic([500121,50074,50072,50076,50133]);
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode in (MfaDenied)
| summarize MfaPrompts=count(), DeniedIPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), FirstDenied=min(Timestamp), LastDenied=max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where MfaPrompts >= 10   // >=10 denied MFA challenges in 5 min = push-bombing / fatigue burst
| join kind=inner (
    AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0 and AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
    | project SuccessTime=Timestamp, AccountUpn, SuccessIP=IPAddress, Country, Application, ClientAppUsed
  ) on AccountUpn
| where SuccessTime between (LastDenied .. LastDenied + 10m)
| project FirstDenied, LastDenied, SuccessTime, AccountUpn, MfaPrompts, DeniedIPs, SuccessIP, Country, Application, ClientAppUsed
| order by MfaPrompts desc
let MfaDenied = dynamic(["500121","50074","50072","50076","50133"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType in (MfaDenied)
| summarize MfaPrompts=count(), DeniedIPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), FirstDenied=min(TimeGenerated), LastDenied=max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where MfaPrompts >= 10   // >=10 denied MFA challenges in 5 min = push-bombing / fatigue burst
| join kind=inner (
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "0" and AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
    | project SuccessTime=TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SuccessIP=IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
  ) on UserPrincipalName
| where SuccessTime between (LastDenied .. LastDenied + 10m)
| project FirstDenied, LastDenied, SuccessTime, UserPrincipalName, MfaPrompts, DeniedIPs, SuccessIP, Location, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| order by MfaPrompts desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:(500121 OR 50074 OR 50072 OR 50076 OR 50133)
