Helpdesk-initiated password reset followed by privileged account remote logon AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the May-2025 Scattered Spider pivot: an actor calls IT helpdesk posing as an employee to reset credentials, then logs into an admin account. Detects an admin/helpdesk resetting SOMEONE ELSE's password, followed within 8h by a remote-interactive successful logon to that account. Rationale: Encodes the article's explicit May-2025 chain — 'called the company's IT helpdesk, posing as employees, to reset credentials and gain access to administrator accounts' — as reset-of-another-user's-password (Actor != Target) followed within 8h by a successful (admin) logon. CISA AA23-320A corroborates helpdesk-impersonation password reset + MFA transfer as core Scattered Spider initial access. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1078.003 T1098 T1556.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit helpdesk password reset for a genuinely locked-out admin who then logs in remotely via VPN
  • Scheduled admin credential rotation followed by the admin re-authenticating
  • New admin onboarding where an existing admin sets the initial password
  • Break-glass account reset during an IR exercise
  • MSP/outsourced IT resetting privileged accounts from their own remote ASN as normal course of business
Suppression filter
| where Actor !in~ ("knownhelpdesk-svc@corp.com") and IPs !has "10."   // tune: exclude sanctioned helpdesk service account and internal VPN egress once baselined
Response runbook
1) Triage: call the account owner out-of-band (NOT via chat/email the attacker may control) to confirm they requested the reset; compare the post-reset logon IP/ASN/Location to the user's baseline. 2) Contain: if unverified, disable the account, revoke sessions/tokens, and re-reset the password through a verified channel; page the helpdesk to confirm caller identity-proofing on the ticket. 3) Hunt: review what the account did after logon (role grants, VPN config, mailbox rules, access to crown-jewel apps) and check the helpdesk queue for other same-day resets from the same requester pattern.
let ResetWindow = 8h;
let Resets = IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(3d)
| where ActionType in ("Account Password Changed","Account Password Reset","Recover password")
| where isnotempty(TargetAccountUpn) and AccountUpn != TargetAccountUpn   // someone resetting ANOTHER user's password (helpdesk pattern)
| project ResetTime=Timestamp, TargetUpn=TargetAccountUpn, Actor=AccountUpn;
Resets
| join kind=inner (
    IdentityLogonEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(3d)
    | where ActionType == "LogonSuccess" and LogonType in ("RemoteInteractive","Network","Interactive")
    | project LogonTime=Timestamp, TargetUpn=AccountUpn, IPAddress, DeviceName, LogonType
  ) on TargetUpn
| where LogonTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + ResetWindow)
| summarize LogonCount=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), Devices=make_set(DeviceName,10), FirstLogon=min(LogonTime) by ResetTime, TargetUpn, Actor
| order by ResetTime desc
let ResetWindow = 8h;
let Resets = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
| where OperationName in ("Reset password (by admin)","Reset user password","Change user password")
| where Result == "success"
| mv-expand TargetResources
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources.userPrincipalName)
| extend Actor = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy.user)).userPrincipalName)
| where isnotempty(TargetUpn)
| project ResetTime=TimeGenerated, TargetUpn, Actor;
Resets
| join kind=inner (
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | project LogonTime=TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, AutonomousSystemNumber
  ) on $left.TargetUpn == $right.UserPrincipalName
| where LogonTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + ResetWindow)
| join kind=inner (
    IdentityInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | extend Roles = tostring(AssignedRoles)
    | where Roles has "Admin"
    | summarize by AccountUPN
  ) on $left.TargetUpn == $right.AccountUPN
| summarize LogonCount=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), ASNs=make_set(AutonomousSystemNumber,10), FirstLogon=min(LogonTime) by ResetTime, TargetUpn, Actor
| order by ResetTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("Reset password (by admin)" OR "Reset user password" OR "Change user password")

Genymotion/Genymobile Android emulator execution on a corporate endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the article's specific tooling: 'they commonly use the Genymobile Android emulator during their MFA attacks.' Detects execution of Genymotion desktop/CLI binaries or any process signed by Genymobile on a Windows endpoint, used to receive push/SMS OTPs on an attacker-controlled virtual device. Rationale: Uses the article's named tool 'Genymobile Android emulator' — pivots on the Genymobile\Genymotion install path plus signer company 'Genymobile' (the high-fidelity anchor that separates attacker use from the generic name player.exe). Signer-based match keeps it article-specific rather than a generic emulator template. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1564.006 T1621
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mobile app dev/QA engineers legitimately running Genymotion for Android testing
  • Automated CI runners with Genymotion Cloud/Desktop for app test pipelines
  • Support staff reproducing a mobile app bug in an emulator
  • Security researchers analyzing Android malware in Genymotion
  • Sales-engineering demo machines running the mobile app in an emulator
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("dev-qa-host01","mobileqa-ci01") and AccountName !in~ ("mobiledev","qa-runner")   // baseline out sanctioned mobile-dev hosts/users
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host/user belongs to a mobile-dev/QA cost centre — if not, treat as suspicious; capture install time, parent process, and download source of the emulator binary. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host and, if the user is non-dev, disable their account and revoke MFA tokens, since the emulator is likely staging a rogue MFA device. 3) Hunt: correlate this host/user with the MFA push-bombing detection and helpdesk-reset detection; check for a fresh MFA method registration in Entra AuditLogs within +/-24h and outbound connections from the emulator to auth/OTP endpoints.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("genymotion.exe","gmtool.exe","genyshell.exe","genymotion-player.exe","player.exe") and FolderPath has @"\Genymobile\Genymotion\")
     or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Genymobile"
     or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Genymobile"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where (ActingProcessName has_any ("genymotion.exe","gmtool.exe","genyshell.exe","genymotion-player.exe","player.exe") and ActingProcessName has @"\Genymobile\Genymotion\")
     or ActingProcessFileCompany has "Genymobile"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DragonForce encryptor bulk file encryption (Scattered Spider impact) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the impact phase named in the article: Scattered Spider 'deployed DragonForce encryptor in ransomware attacks against UK retail companies.' Detects the DragonForce-specific encrypted-file extensions being written in bulk by a single process, plus the readme.txt ransom note pattern. Rationale: Anchors on DragonForce-specific encrypted-file extensions (.dragonforce_encrypted / .df_win / .dragonforce) confirmed across Group-IB, Trend Micro and Darktrace write-ups, gated by a bulk >=25-file-per-process threshold to isolate mass encryption from a stray single file. Extension is the malware-family IOC, keeping this specific to the article's named encryptor rather than generic ransomware. Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/dragonforce-ransomware/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/security/news/ransomware-spotlight/ransomware-spotlight-dragonforce • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/tracking-a-dragon-investigating-a-dragonforce-affiliated-ransomware-attack-with-darktrace
ATT&CKT1486 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team detonating a DragonForce sample in an isolated sandbox/malware-analysis VM
  • Backup/restore test that rehydrates previously-encrypted files carrying the extension
  • Threat-intel analyst copying IOC sample files with these extensions onto a share
  • Red-team ransomware simulation using DragonForce-mimicking extensions
  • IR imaging that reintroduces encrypted artifacts from a prior incident
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("malware-sandbox01","ir-analysis-vm") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Analysis\"   // exclude sanctioned detonation hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcess (name/SHA256/path) writing the extensions and the write rate — a single process crossing 25 files across many folders in minutes is a live encryptor; confirm the host isn't a sanctioned malware-analysis VM. 2) Contain: immediately network-isolate the host, kill/quarantine the InitiatingProcess and its SHA256 org-wide, and disable the executing account; check for the paired BYOVD driver load used by DragonForce to kill EDR. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same InitiatingProcessSHA256 and readme.txt drops in inetpub/wwwroot across the fleet, look for prior data-staging/exfil (e.g. SSH to external IPs) and shadow-copy deletion, and pivot to the initial-access accounts flagged by the MFA/helpdesk detections.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName endswith ".dragonforce_encrypted" or FileName endswith ".df_win" or FileName endswith ".dragonforce"
| summarize FileCount=count(), Folders=dcount(FolderPath), SampleFile=any(FileName), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where FileCount >= 25   // bulk sequential encryption by a single process
| order by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".dragonforce_encrypted" or TargetFileName endswith ".df_win" or TargetFileName endswith ".dragonforce"
| summarize FileCount=count(), Folders=dcount(TargetFilePath), SampleFile=any(TargetFileName), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| where FileCount >= 25   // bulk sequential encryption by a single process
| order by FileCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MFA fatigue / push-bombing Actions on Objectives High
Many MFA pushes to same user in short window — suggests adversary attempting approval-fatigue.
ATT&CKT1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication AADSignInEventsBeta
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode in (50074, 50076, 50158, 50125, 50097)
| extend MfaPrompt = AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
| where MfaPrompt
| summarize attempts = count(), distinct_ips = dcount(IPAddress)
    by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where attempts > 10
| order by attempts desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType == 50158        // MFA Challenge required / failed
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen  = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs       = make_set(IPAddress, 5)
            by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Attempts > 3               // tune to baseline
| order by Attempts desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Authentication.action="failure" AND Authentication.signature="*MFA*"
    by _time span=5m, Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where count > 10

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where count > 10

External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent

    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where Account !endswith "$"

FortiClient EMS exploit chain (CVE-2026-35616) deploying EKZ Infostealer via fortitray/ipsec → PowerShell AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-35616 post-exploitation chain where a compromised FortiClient EMS drives the client processes fortitray.exe/ipsec.exe to spawn cmd/PowerShell that stages a CMD script under the FortiClient Trace logs and launches the fake 'FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe' patch payload. Article-specific because Fortinet client binaries never legitimately spawn shells or run a payload named FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE-2026-35616 process tree confirmed by Arctic Wolf (fortitray.exe/ipsec.exe → cmd → powershell → FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe) plus the unique CMD staging path C:\Program Files\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\{GUID}.cmd. Fortinet client binaries spawning shells is inherently anomalous, making this very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-forticlient-ems-flaw-to-push-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FortiClient auto-update writing scripts to the Trace\scripts directory during a genuine patch cycle
  • Administrator manually running cmd/PowerShell diagnostics while FortiClient tray is the foreground process (rare parent attribution)
  • EDR/AV response tooling quarantining a file named similarly to the payload
  • Security team detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("FortiClient\\FortiSSLVPNclient","FortiUpdate") and not(ProcessCommandLine has "FortiEndpoint_Patch"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm fortitray.exe/ipsec.exe → cmd → powershell parentage and whether FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe (SHA256 0da123adf9...) executed; decode any base64 PowerShell in InitiatingProcessCommandLine. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the payload process, block hash 0da123adf9... and IP 83.138.53.110, and take the FortiClient EMS server offline for patching (CVE-2026-35616). 3) Hunt: sweep all EMS-managed endpoints for the same parent chain, the Trace\scripts drop, C:\ProgramData\log.txt, and outbound traffic to 83.138.53.110.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("fortitray.exe","ipsec.exe") and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe"))
    or FileName =~ "FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName has_any ("fortitray.exe","ipsec.exe") and NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe"))
    or NewProcessName has "FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe"
    or CommandLine has @"\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FortiClient EMS Exploit Chain Deploying EKZ Infostealer (CVE-2026-35616)
id: 6b1f2a44-4d31-4d2e-9f0c-2a1e8c7b9d01
description: Detects FortiClient client binaries spawning a shell or the fake FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe payload, consistent with CVE-2026-35616 exploitation delivering EKZ Infostealer.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fortibleed-credential-theft-linked-to.html
  - https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent_shell:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\fortitray.exe'
      - '\ipsec.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
  payload:
    Image|endswith: '\FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe'
  staging:
    CommandLine|contains: '\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\'
  condition: parent_shell or payload or staging
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@ParentImage:(*\fortitray.exe OR *\Fortitray.exe OR *\ipsec.exe OR *\IPSec.exe) AND @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\Cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe)) OR @Image:(*\FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe OR *\fortiendpoint_patch.exe) OR @CommandLine:*\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ParentBaseFileName=/(fortitray|ipsec)\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell)\.exe$/i) OR ImageFileName=/FortiEndpoint_Patch\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/\\Fortinet\\FortiClient\\logs\\Trace\\scripts\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ( (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("fortitray.exe","ipsec.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe")) OR Processes.process_name="FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe" OR Processes.process="*\\Fortinet\\FortiClient\\logs\\Trace\\scripts\\*" ) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ( (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("fortitray.exe","ipsec.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe")) OR Processes.process_name="FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe" OR Processes.process="*\\Fortinet\\FortiClient\\logs\\Trace\\scripts\\*" ) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
EKZ Infostealer C2 download and HTTP-POST exfiltration to 83.138.53.110 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network egress to the FortiBleed/EKZ C2 host 83.138.53.110, including the payload pull at /dl/p.exe and credential exfil POST to /service/save.php. Article-specific because these exact URI paths and the C2 IP are tied to the EKZ Infostealer campaign, not a generic beacon template. Rationale: 83.138.53.110 with URIs /dl/p.exe and /service/save.php is the confirmed EKZ download+exfil endpoint (Arctic Wolf). The two additional IPs are article-listed FortiBleed infrastructure (likely Tor exits — hence lower confidence on those two), so the primary alert weight is on the second-source-confirmed 83.138.53.110. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/fortibleed-attackers-firewalls-credentials-stealers
ATT&CKT1105 T1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or research hosts intentionally connecting to 83.138.53.110 for sample retrieval
  • Tor exit nodes 185.220.101.15 / 192.42.116.14 being contacted for legitimate Tor usage in the environment
  • Security scanners/crawlers touching the C2 IP during internet-wide scans
  • Sinkhole or takedown infrastructure now resolving to the same IP
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName driving the connection — powershell.exe or FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe reaching 83.138.53.110 confirms EKZ; check for the /service/save.php POST indicating data left the host. 2) Contain: block 83.138.53.110 at proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat any credentials on it (especially browser-stored) as compromised → force password resets. 3) Hunt: pivot on all hosts that resolved/connected to the IP, correlate with FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe execution and C:\ProgramData\log.txt creation to scope the intrusion.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("83.138.53.110","185.220.101.15","192.42.116.14")
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("/dl/p.exe","/service/save.php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("83.138.53.110","185.220.101.15","192.42.116.14")
    or RequestURL has_any ("/dl/p.exe","/service/save.php")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EKZ Infostealer browser credential theft and staging to C:\ProgramData\log.txt AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts EKZ Infostealer credential collection: a non-browser process touching Chrome 'Local State'/'Login Data' and Firefox key4.db/logins.json/cookies.sqlite, plus creation of the exact exfil staging file C:\ProgramData\log.txt. Article-specific because the staging path and the FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe/PowerShell writer tie directly to the EKZ chain. Rationale: C:\ProgramData\log.txt is the exact EKZ staging file Arctic Wolf documented, and the browser secret stores (Chrome Local State/Login Data, Firefox key4.db/logins.json/cookies.sqlite) are the confirmed harvesting targets. Binding the file writes to the FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe/PowerShell writer keeps this tight to the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/05/29/forticlient-ems-vulnerability-infostealer/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/sync software copying browser profile databases (key4.db, Login Data)
  • Browser-migration or password-manager import tools accessing Login Data / logins.json
  • A benign application coincidentally writing C:\ProgramData\log.txt (common generic log filename)
  • Endpoint DLP or forensic collection agents reading browser credential stores
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","backup.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\Application\", @"\Mozilla Firefox\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writer of C:\ProgramData\log.txt is FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe/PowerShell (not a legit app) and check whether browser secret stores were touched in the same session. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture C:\ProgramData\log.txt for scoping, and force-reset all browser-saved and SSO credentials for the user (assume cookies/session tokens stolen → revoke sessions). 3) Hunt: look for the follow-on POST to 83.138.53.110/service/save.php and repeat the file-staging query org-wide across EMS-managed endpoints.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath =~ @"C:\ProgramData\log.txt" and ActionType == "FileCreated")
    or (FileName in~ ("key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Login Data","Local State")
        and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe","p.exe","powershell.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFilePath =~ @"C:\ProgramData\log.txt" and EventType == "FileCreated")
    or (TargetFileName in~ ("key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Login Data","Local State")
        and ActingProcessName has_any ("FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe","p.exe","powershell.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EKZ Infostealer / FortiBleed known-bad file hash execution sweep AIInstallation Medium
Retrospective IOC sweep for execution or on-disk presence of the EKZ Infostealer payload by the exact SHA256/SHA1/MD5 published for the FortiBleed campaign. Article-specific: these are the concrete hashes tied to the fake FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe / p.exe payload. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the published EKZ payload hashes. SHA256 0da123adf9..., SHA1 17e771..., and MD5 338662... are second-source confirmed by Arctic Wolf as the FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe payload; the remaining four SHA256 are article-listed campaign samples included for retro sweep. Hash matches are effectively zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/forticlient-code-execution-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A malware analyst intentionally detonating the sample in a managed environment
  • Hash collision is not realistic for SHA256 — near-zero false positives
  • EDR quarantine copy of the file being re-scanned and matching the hash
  • Threat-intel enrichment pipeline re-hashing a stored artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the match host and whether it was process execution (active infection) vs. a dormant file drop; capture full path and initiating command line. 2) Contain: isolate host, block all listed hashes in EDR, and quarantine the artifact; assume EKZ ran → treat local credentials as compromised. 3) Hunt: expand to the process-tree, C2 (83.138.53.110), and staging-file detections; check the FortiClient EMS server for CVE-2026-35616 exploitation as the entry point.

    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 in~ (Sha256) or SHA1 =~ "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f" or MD5 =~ "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081"
    | extend Evt="ProcessCreated", Cmd=ProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)

    | extend Evt=ActionType, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Evt, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1, MD5, Cmd
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DeviceProcessEvents

SecurityEvent

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:

            - '-NoProfile'

      cross-shell escaping
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081") or SHA1 in~ ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081") or MD5 in~ ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081") or SHA1 in~ ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081") or MD5 in~ ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.process_hash IN ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.process_hash IN ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e", "d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a", "fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5", "2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2", "2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff", "17e771c78430cc67e71d4547f8996a1a488e9d3f", "338662fd0c4d750a0ba203a32b59f081")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
Critical

New ChocoPoC RAT Targets Vulnerability Researchers via Fake PoC Exploit Repos

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 15 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Attackers are hiding a data-stealing trojan inside fake exploit code aimed at the people who hunt bugs for a living. The malware, called ChocoPoC, travels in Python proof-of-concept (PoC) repositories on GitHub that claim to exploit hot new CVEs. Run one, and it quietly lifts your saved passwords, browser cookies, and files, then hands the attacker a shell on your machine.&nbsp;YesWeHack and

IPs91.132.163.78
